# 207. Lambda@Edge & CloudFront Functions
# Section: Serverless Overviews from a Solution Architect Perspective
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/16256236
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about
Customization At The Edge.
So what does it mean?
Well we know we deploy our functions
and our applications in a specific region,
but sometimes using, for example, CloudFront,
we have the Edge locations are distributing our content.
And sometimes the modern applications require
to execute some form of logic at the Edge
before reaching the application itself.
So these are called Edge Functions,
and this is a piece of code that you write
and that you will attach to your CloudFront distributions.
The idea is that you want to run these functions
close to users in order to minimize latency in some cases.
So CloudFront has two kinds of functions,
you have the CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge.
The idea will be to be able to understand
when they are required and their differences,
and will do this in this lecture.
But using the Edge Functions,
you don't have to manage any servers,
these Edge Functions are deployed globally.
And the use cases of them,
for example, would be to customize the CDN content
coming out of CloudFront.
Also, you only pay for what you use,
and it is fully serverless.
So now let's have a deeper look
into these things, the use cases.
The first one is around website security and privacy,
then we have dynamic web applications at the Edge,
we can do search engine optimization, SEO,
we can do intelligent routing across
Origins and data center,
Bot mitigation at the Edge,
real-time image transformation at the Edge,
A/B testing, user authentication and authorization,
user prioritization, user tracking and analytics, and so on.
So this is a lot of different customizations
we can have using CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge.
So now let's discuss what CloudFront Functions
are used for and how they work.
So this is what a typical request
into CloudFront looks like.
So the client will do a request into CloudFront,
and this is called a viewer request,
because the client views it.
Then CloudFront will do an origin request
into your origin server,
the server will reply to CloudFront,
so we have an origin response,
and finally CloudFront sends that response to the client,
so we have a viewer response.
Now CloudFront Functions are lightweight functions
written in JavaScript,
and they modified the viewer request and response.
They're used for high-scale,
latency-sensitive CDN customizations,
which gives you sub-millisecond startup times,
and a scale of millions of requests per second.
As I said, they're used to change viewer request
and responses only,
so the view request is after CloudFront
receives a request from a viewer, we can modify this,
or the viewer response is to
before CloudFront forwards the response back to the viewer.
It's a native feature of CloudFront,
and the entire code is managed
from within CloudFront directly.
Remember, CloudFront Functions high performance,
high scale only for the viewer request and response.
Now Lambda@Edge is a bit more,
so you can modify all of them.
So these are functions returned in NodeJS or Python,
and you scale to 1000s of requests per second,
and it's used to change CloudFront request
and response, multiple ones, so all of them actually,
the viewer request and the origin request,
which is before CloudFront forwards a request to the origin.
You also have the origin response,
which is after CloudFront receives the response
from the origin, and the viewer response,
which is before CloudFront forwards
the response back to the viewer.
You author your function in one region,
which is us-east-1, which is the same region
where you manage your CloudFront distributions,
and then CloudFront is going to replicate this function
to all of its locations.
So we have a table here to differentiate
between CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge.
So one notable difference is the runtime support,
of course JavaScript only for CloudFront Functions,
and then NodeJS and Python for Lambda@Edge.
The scale is really, really high scale
for CloudFront Functions, we're talking about
millions of requests per second,
versus thousands for Lambda@Edge.
Now where the trigger is happening is a big difference.
So Lambda@Edge has impact on both
the viewer request and the origin,
whereas the CloudFront Functions is only on the viewer.
And very important, the max execution time
is less than one millisecond for CloudFront Functions,
so they're very, very quick and simple functions.
Whereas for Lambda@Edge you can get
up to 5 to 10 seconds,
so you can perform a lot of logic in these functions.
The rest, you can have a look, okay?
Now in terms of use cases,
CloudFront Functions is going to be for
cache key normalization,
so to transform, for example the request attributes
to create an optimal cache key.
Header manipulation to insert, modify, or delete
HTTP headers in the request or response,
or to do URL rewrites or redirects,
or to request of an authorization
to create and validate JWT tokens to allow or deny request.
So all these things can be executed
in less than one millisecond,
whereas Lambda@Edge has a longer execution time,
it could be up to 10 seconds, for example.
You have adjustable CPU and memory,
so you can load a lot of libraries,
and your code can depend therefore,
on third party libraries, such as the SDK
if you wanted to access other AWS services.
You also have network access to external services

so you can really perform some big integrations.
And Lambd@Edge gives you file system access,
or access to the body itself of the HTTP request,
so you can do some more customizations.

# 208. Lambda in VPC
# Section: Serverless Overviews from a Solution Architect Perspective
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/33878800
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's talk
about some networking fundamentals for Lambda.
So by default, when you launch your functions
they're launched outside of your own VPC.
They're actually launched in an AWS own VPC.
So you do not have access to resources within your VPC.
So if you launch an RDS database, an ElastiCache Cache,
or an internal load balancer
then your Lambda function will not have access to it.
So this is the default Lambda deployment.
It will work if it needs to access any
public API on the internet.
It will work if it needs to access DynamoDB
because DynamoDB is a public resource on the AWS cloud.
But if you have a private RDS database,
the connectivity will not be working.
You know where this is getting to
we need to actually launch your Lambda function in your VPC.
So this is an option you can do
and you need to specify therefore, your VPC ID,
the subnets you want to launch in,
and attach a security group to your Lambda function.
Then your Lambda will have a elastic network interface
in your subnets, and therefore it will be able to
access your Amazon RDS, for example, running in your VPC.
So this is how we launch a Lambda function
in your private subnets.
And therefore you will have private connectivity
to anything in your VPC, which is good.
So a major use case of Lambda in a VPC
is to use Lambda with the RDS proxy.
So again, we have an RDS database in a private subnet
but we have our Lambda functions
and they access it directly.
But the problem is that
if they access your RDS database directly
it's going to be huge problem,
because if you have many of the functions
appearing and disappearing over time,
then you may have too many open connections
under high load on your RDS database
and it will lead to timeouts and issues.
So instead, what you would do is to launch an RDS proxy
and this proxy was going to pull connection and connect
with less connections into your RDS database instance.
So your Lambda functions now connect to the RDS proxy
which connects to the RDS database instance
and you've solved your architectural problems.
So three benefits of the RDS proxy is that number one
it improves scalability
by pulling and sharing database connections.
Also, in case of a failover,
this will improve the availability by reducing by 66%
the failover time and preserving connections.
This is for RDS and Aurora, of course.
And also if you wanted to enforce IAM authentication
you could enforce it at the RDS proxy level
and store these details in secrets manager.
So for this to work for the Lambda functions
to connect to your RDS proxy,
you need to launch your Lambda functions in your VPC,
if that makes sense,
because your RDS proxy is never publicly accessible.
And therefore, if you launch your Lambda functions publicly
you will have no network connectivity
to your RDS proxy because it is never public.
So if you understand this
you will be able to solve one or two questions at the exam.
Okay, that's it.
I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# Section: Serverless Overviews from a Solution Architect Perspective

# Caption: en_US (manual)

Is there a tight integration from RDS, Aurora, and Lambda?
Well, we can actually invoke Lambda functions
from within your database instance in some cases.
And this would allow you to actually process data events
happening from within your database.
So this is supported, for example,
by RDS for PostgreSQL, and Aurora MySQL.
And the idea is that, for example,
a user is going to insert an event data into your table,
your registration table.
And RDS will be set up
to directly invoke your Lambda function.
Your Lambda function may send a welcome email to your user,
and then the user will receive it.
This is something that you have to set up
from within the database by connecting to it.
This is not something that you set up from the AWS console.
And when you do do that
the RDS instance is the one invoking your Lambda function.
And so therefore you must sure to have allowed
the inbound traffic from the RDS database instance
to the Lambda function through whatever way,
either because your Lambda is on the public interest.
So we can use the Invoke,
or the NAT gateway, or the VPC endpoints and so on.
But network connectivity is important.
On top of it, of course,
because your RDS database instance is going to
invoke your Lambda function,
then you must have the required permissions
to invoke the Lambda function.
And so you make sure that your database instance
has a proper IAM policy.
This is completely different
from using the RDS event notifications.
So these notifications are happening within AWS
and there are notifications that tell you information
about the database instance itself.
For example, when it was created,
when it was started, and so on.
And you don't have any information
of the data happening within your database.
So don't fall for this trap.
You can subscribe, for example,
to events about your database instance,
your database snapshots, your parameter group,
your security group, your proxy,
or the custom engine version.
But you're not gonna get information
about the data within your database.
You get near real time events,
so up to five minutes of delivery.
And then you can send these to SNS,
or you can also intercept them in EventBridge.
So from SNS, we can, for example,
send them to an SQS Queue, or a Lambda function.
And from Event Bridge
you can have so many different destinations,
including, for example, a Lambda function.
But remember, you do not get information
about the data events themselves.
You have to use the previous methodology
as I've shown you from before.
Okay, that's it for this lecture,

So now let's talk about a database

which is Amazon DynamoDB.
So it's a fully managed database, it's highly available,
and it has replication of data across multiple AZs.
DynamoDB is special because it is Cloud native,

So it's not a relational database like RDS and Aurora
although it has still transaction supports.
So with DynamoDB, the use case is that
you can scale to massive workloads
because the database is internally distributed.
That means you can scale
to millions of requests per seconds,
trillions of rows and hundreds of terabytes of storage.
The idea is that, and you need to remember this,
you have single digit millisecond performance
which is going to be fast, of course, and consistent.
Also for all your security needs,
everything is integrated with IAM.
So for security, authorization, and administration,
it's low cost, has auto-scaling capabilities
that we'll see in a second,
and there is no maintenance or patching,
it's always available.
So you don't need to provision a database,
it's already there.
You just need to go ahead and create a table
and say how much capacity you want to put in this table.
You have two kind of table class,
you have the standard class for frequently accessed data
and you have the infrequent access,
the IA table class for infrequently accessed data.
So the basics of DynamoDB is that
DynamoDB is made of tables
but you don't need to create a database, okay?
It's not like Aurora and RDS,
the database is already there,
that is the service named DynamoDB.
So you go ahead and you create tables
and each table will have a primary key
and you decide on this at the creation time,
and then you add data.
So each table can have an infinite number of items
and there are rows and each item will have attributes.
And they're pretty much columns, but you can add
the attributes over time and they can be null.
So this is a big difference in an RDS or Aurora database,
you can add columns over time, but it's complicated process
and it can be difficult to evolve your schemas.
But then in DynamoDB, you can add attributes just like that
over time without any pre-requirements.
So the item size, the maximum item size in DynamoDB
is 400 kilobytes,
so DynamoDB is not there to store very large objects.
You have different data types supported,
you have the Scalar types such as String, Number, Binary,
Boolean, and Null, you have list, and maps, and sets.
So DynamoDB is at the exam,
gonna be a great choice if you need to see from
the exam that the schema,
so that means how your data looks, how it's shaped,
if the schema needs to rapidly evolve.
In that case, DynamoDB is a much better choice
than Aurora or RDS,
so look for this at the exam.
So here is an example of a table in DynamoDB.
We have a partition key,
optionally a sort key, which composes your primary key,
and then we have attributes
and then it looks just like a database, okay?
But it's possible, for example,
for your attributes to be null or to add attributes
over time, which makes the strength of DynamoDB.
Another thing you need to choose,
if you need to choose DynamoDB
is the capacity mode for reads and writes.
So you can control how to manage your table's capacity
and there are two modes you need to know about.
There is the provision mode, which is the default
in which you are going to provision the capacity in advance,
so you're going to say how many reads
and writes you expect per second
and that's going to be your capacity of your table,
so you need to plan the capacity beforehand
and then you're going to pay for every provision RCU or WCU
which stands for Read Capacity Units
or Write Capacity Units.
Although if you want a planned capacity,
you can still automatically adjust it
thanks to autoscaling,
which will increase or decrease your RCU and WCU
over time based on the load of your table.
So this is the provision mode and it works great
if your load is predictable, it evolves smoothly,
and you wanna do some cost saving
but there is also the On-Demand Mode.
And here, the read and writes capacity
will scale automatically with your workload.
There's no capacity planning needed,
there is actually no concept of RCU and WCU,
so instead in the On-Demand Mode
you're going to pay exactly for what you use,
so for every single writes
and every single reads you're going to pay for it.
So it's a lot more expensive as a solution
but it's going to be amazing for unpredictable workloads
or workloads that have steep, sudden spikes.
So again, these are some keywords you need to look
at for the exam,
if you have an application that will scale
from a thousand transactions
to 1 million transactions in less than a minute,
Provision Mode is not going to be good for you
because it doesn't scale fast enough.
So in that case, you need to use On-Demand Mode
or if you have a workload that has no transactions at all,
maybe four or five times a day maximum then
On-Demand Mode is great because you're only going to pay
for these four or five transactions.
So look out for the differences and these keywords
and you will be able to select
between Provision Mode and On-Demand Mode.
So that's it for the DynamoDB basics,
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 212. Amazon DynamoDB - Advanced Features
# Section: Serverless Overviews from a Solution Architect Perspective
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13672550
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about the advanced features
that can come up at the exam for DynamoDB.
And the first one is DynamoDB Accelerator or DAX.
So this is a fully-managed, highly available,
and seamless in-memory cache for DynamoDB.
The idea is that if you have a lot of reads
on your DynamoDB table,
then you can create a DAX cluster
to solve read congestion by caching the data.
And with DynamoDB DAX,
you get microseconds latency for cached data.
So this is something you have to look out for
in terms of keywords at the exam.
It doesn't require for you
to change any of your application logic
because the DAX cluster is compatible
with the existing DynamoDB APIs.
So you have your DynamoDB tables and your application,
and you will just create a DAX cluster
made of few cache nodes, connect to this DAX cluster.
And then behind the scenes,
the DAX cluster is connected to your Amazon DynamoDB table.
The cache has a default TTL of five minutes,
but you can change this.
So you may ask me,
why should I use DAX and not elastic cache?
Well, DAX is in front of DynamoDB
and it's going to be very helpful
for individual objects cache or queries,
and scanned queries' cache.
But if you want to store, say, aggregation results,
then Amazon ElastiCache is a great way to do it.
So if you want to store a very big computation
that you've done on top of Amazon DynamoDB.
So they're not drop-in replacements for one another,
they're actually complementary.
But most of the time,
for caching solution on top of Amazon DynamoDB,
it's just going to be using DynamoDB Accelerator DAX.
You can also do stream processing on top of DynamoDB.
The idea is that you want to have a stream
of all the modifications that happen on your table.
Would it be create, update, and delete.
And the use cases for that will be, for example,
to react to changes on your DynamoDB table in real time.
For example, to send a welcome email
whenever you have a new user in your user's table.
Or if so, you may wanna do real-time usage analytics,
or maybe you want to insert data into a derivative table,
or you want to implement cross region replication,
or you want to invoke Lambda on any changes made
on your DynamoDB table.
So two kind of stream processing on DynamoDB.
You have DynamoDB Streams, with 24 hours retention,
a limited number of consumers,
and is going to be greatly used with Lambda triggers.
Or if you wanted to read it yourself,
there is something
called the DynamoDB Stream Kinesis Adapter.
Or you can also choose to send all your changes
directly into a Kinesis Data Streams.
And here you can have up to one year of retention,
you can have a much higher number of consumers,
and you have a much higher number
of ways to process the data,
whether we blend the functions, Kinesis Data Analytics,
Kinesis Data Firehose, Glue Streaming ETLs, and so on.
So let's have a look at an architectural diagram
to understand DynamoDB Streams better.
So your application does create updates
and delete operations on top of your DynamoDB table,
which is going to be either a DynamoDB Streams
or a Kinesis Data Streams.
If you choose to use Kinesis Data Streams,
then you can use Kinesis Data Firehose.
And from this, you can send your data into Amazon Redshift
for analytics purposes,
or Amazon S3 if you want to archive some of the data,
or Amazon OpenSearch to do some indexing
and some searches on top of it.
Or if you are using DynamoDB Streams,
you can have a processing layer
and you can use either the DynamoDB KCL Adapter
to run your applications
on top of EC2 instances or Lambda functions.
And from there, do some notifications on top of SNS
or do some filtering and transformations
into another DynamoDB table.
Or use the processing layer to do whatever you want,
such as, again, send the data to Amazon OpenSearch.
So I didn't represent all the possibilities
or our architectures.
Of course, you can have EC22 instances
reading from Kinesis Data Streams.
You can have Kinesis Data Analytics and so on
on top of Kinesis Data Streams, many, many transformations.
But again, you know enough now
to figure out what is going to be the right architecture
at the right time.
DynamoDB also has a concept of global table.
So a global table is a table, of course,
that is going to be replicated across multiple regions.
So you can have a table in US-East-1
and a table in AP-Southeast-2.
And there is a two-way replication between the tables.
That means that you can write to a table
either in US-East-1 and AP-Southeast-2.
So here, the idea with global tables
is to make DynamoDB accessible
with low latency in multiple regions.
And it is an Active-Active replication.
That means that your applications can read and write
to the table in any specific region.
And to enable global tables,
you must first enable DynamoDB Streams
because this is the underlying infrastructure
to replicate the table across regions.
DynamoDB also has a feature named Time To Live, or TTL.
The idea is that you want to automatically delete items
after an expiry timestamp.
So you have your table, SessionData,
and then you will have one last attribute
called ExpTime, which is your TTL,
and it has a timestamp in it.
And the idea is that you're going to define a TTL.
And as soon as the current time in the Epoch timestamp
is going to be over your ExpTime column,
then automatically it's going to expire items
and then eventually delete them through a deletion process.
So the idea is that the items in your data table
are going to be deleted after a while.
So the use cases for this will be to only store data
by keeping only the most current items
or to adhere to regulatory obligations by,
for example, deleting data after two years.
Or another use case that is very common at the exam
is the web session handling.
So a user would log into your website,
and then would've a session.
And you would keep the session in a central place,
such as DynamoDB for two hours.
And you would set the session data there
and any kind of applications can access it.
And at some point, after two hours,
if it hasn't been renewed,
then it will expire and move away from this table.
You can also use DynamoDB for disaster recovery.
So what are your backups options?
Well, you can have continuous backups
with point-in-time recovery, PITR.
So it's optionally enabled,
but you can have it for the last 35 days.
And then if you enable it,
you can do a point-in-time recovery
to any time within the backup window.
And if you do happen to do a recovery,
then it will create a new table.
If you wanted to have longer term backups,
then you can use on-demand backups,
and they will be retained until you delete them explicitly.
And doing these kind of backups
do not affect the performance
or the latency of your DynamoDB table.
And if you wanted to have
a better management of your backups,
you can use the AWS Backup Service,
and this will enable you to have lifecycle policies
for your backups and so on.
And also copy your backups across regions
for disaster recovery purposes.
And again, if you were to do a recovery
of one of these backups, it will create a new table.
Now, let's talk about the integrations
between DynamoDB and Amazon S3.
So you can export a table into S3, just like this.
And to do so, you must enable point-in-time recovery
and you would export DynamoDB table into S3.
For example, if you wanted to do some queries,
for example, using the Amazon Athena engine.
So you can export at any point in time
during the last 35 days
because you've enabled continuous backups.
And when you do an export,
this does not affect the read capacity of your table
or your performance.
So with this, you can perform,
for example, data analysis on top of DynamoDB
through exporting through Amazon S3 first.
You can also use this to retain snapshots for auditing,
or to do any kind of big transformation,
maybe any ETL of the data before importing it back
into a new DynamoDB table, for example.
The format of the export can be in DynamoDB JSON
or the ION format.
And similarly, you can import to Amazon S3.
So you can export from S3 into the CSV, JSON, or ION format
back into a new DynamoDB table.
And this does not consume any write capacity
and it will create a new table.
If there are any import errors,
they will be logged in CloudWatch Logs.
So that's it for DynamoDB. I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# 213. API Gateway Overview
# Section: Serverless Overviews from a Solution Architect Perspective
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528488
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So, so far in our serverless journey,
we've seen how to create Lambda functions
and we've seen how to use DynamoDB.
And so the functions can use DynamoDB
as a database for our API, and we can do create, read,
update, delete on our tables,
but we'd like our clients to be able to invoke
this Lambda function in some way.
So there are multiple of doing it.
We can have the client directly invoke the Lambda function,
but that means that the client would need IAM permissions,
or we've seen we can use an application load balancer
to have it in between the client and the Lambda function
and that would expose our Lambda function
as an HTTP endpoint.
There's one last thing we can use.
It's called the API Gateway.
And this is a serverless offering from AWS
which allows us to create REST APIs
that are going to be public and accessible for our clients.
So the client will talk to the API Gateway
and the beautiful things that the API Gateway
will then proxy the request to our Lambda functions.
So it would use an API Gateway
because it provides us more than just an HTTP endpoint.
It will provide us a lot of features
as we'll see in this section,
such as authentication, such as usage plans,
development stages and all that kind of things.
So the API Gateway has a lot of features
and this is just an overview,
but we can integrate the API Gateway and Lambda
and that gives us a full serverless application.
So no infrastructure to manage.
We have support for the WebSocket Protocol
so we can do real-time streaming
through the API Gateway in two different ways.
The API Gateway handle API versioning.
So we can go from version one to version two
and version three and not break our clients.
We can handle multiple environments
that includes a dev, a test and the prod environment.
There is a whole thing about API Gateway and security.
So there's a tons of way to enable security
on your API Gateway
for both authentication and authorization.
We have the ability to create API keys,
do request throttling in case some clients
are doing too many requests on our API Gateway,
and we can also use some common standards
such as Swagger or Open API 3.0
to import quickly defined APIs,
and also we can export them as Swagger and Open API.
We can transform and validate request and response
in the API Gateway level
to ensure that the invocation are correct,
and we can generate SDK and API specifications
and cache API responses.
So lots of features that come with the API Gateway
that are not necessarily included
when you use something as simple
as an application load balancer.
So what is the API Gateway integrate with?
Well, there is a Lambda function
and we've seen this from the previous diagram,
so it can invoke a Lambda function.
And with this integration, it is the most common way
and a very easy way to expose REST a API
backed by a Lambda function
to do a full serverless application.
But also HTTP.
So we can expose any HTTP endpoints in the backend.
So it could be, for example,
an HTTP API you have on premises,
or it could be an application load balancer
you have on your cloud environment.
And why would you do this?
Well, you would use an API Gateway
to leverage the rate limiting features, the caching,
the user authentication, the API keys, et cetera.
So it's definitely used full to have a layer
of API Gateway on top of your HTTP endpoint.
And finally, we can use an evidence service
so we can expose any AWS API through the API Gateway.
So which ones, for example,
where we can start a Step Function workflow,
we can post a message to SQS
directly from an API Gateway API.
Why would you do this?
Well, because maybe you want to add authentication,
deploy some APIs publicly
or do some rate control on some AWS services.
So here is an example of the API Gateway
used with an AWS service.
So example, Kinesis Data Streams.
So we want to have people send data
into a Kinesis Data Streams
but in a secure way,
without giving them access to AWS credentials.
So what we do is that's in between our clients
and our Kinesis Data Streams,
we're going to have the API Gateway.
And the clients will send HTTP request
into the API Gateway.
And it's been configured to then send the messages
into a Kinesis Data Streams.
And as you see in this setting, we don't manage any servers.
Then Kinesis Data Stream from there,
we can, for example, send the records
into a Kinesis Data Firehose
and eventually put them into an Amazon S3 bucket
in the JSON format.
So you start to see the power of API Gateway.
You can actually expose any AWS service
to the outside through an API Gateway.
There are three ways to deploy your API Gateway.
This is called endpoint types.
So the first type, which is the default one
is called Edge-Optimized.
This is for your global clients.
So that means that your API Gateway
is going to be accessible from anywhere in the world.
And to be efficient,
the request are going to be routed
through all the CloudFront Edge locations,
which will improve the latency.
Your API Gateway is still only in one region
where you created it, but it's accessible efficiently
from every CloudFormation Edge location.
Then there's a regional deployment.
So this is when we don't want to use
CloudFront Edge locations.
So it's when we expect all our users
to be within the same region
where we created our API Gateway.
And if you wanted to,
you could create your own platform distribution,
and this will give you the same result
as an Edge-Optimized distribution,
but this time you have more control over location strategies
and the platform settings themselves.
And then finally, the last kind of API Gateway you can do
is a private API Gateway.
So this time it's not public.
So a private API Gateway can only be accessed
from within your VPC.
And it will use interface VPC endpoints for your ENIs.
And to define access to your API Gateway,
you can use a resource policy.
Now, a few comments about the security
on top of the API Gateway.
So you can identify users on the API Gateway
in multiple ways.
The first way is through IAM roles.
So this is very helpful if you have internal applications,
for example, running on EC2 instances,
and they want to access an API on API Gateway,
they can just use IAM roles.
If you wanted to have external users,
for example, for mobile applications or web applications,
then you would use something called Amazon Cognito.
Or if you wanted to implement your own logic,
you could do do so with a custom authorizer.
This is a Lambda function.
Also, you can have HTTPS security
through your own custom domain name
by integration with a service called
the AWS Certificate Manager or ACM.
And so that certificate, if you're using
an Edge-Optimized endpoint must be in us-east-1
but if you're using a regional endpoint
then that certificate may be in the same region
as the API Gateway stage.
Finally, you must set up, of course, a CNAME
or an A-alias record in Route 53
to point to your domain and API Gateway.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# 215. Step Functions
# Section: Serverless Overviews from a Solution Architect Perspective
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13541324
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's learn
about the AWS Step Functions.
So, Step Functions is a way for you
to build a serverless visual workflow
to perform orchestration,
and it's usually of your Lambda functions.
So you would design a graph,
and you would say at each step of the graph,
in case of success or failure, what goes on next?
And this is really cool,
because you can start really having some complex workflows
within AWS.
So Step Functions have some internal features,
such as sequencing, parallel functions, conditions,
timeouts, error handling, and so much.
And it doesn't just do Lambda functions.
It is actually integrate with EC2 instances, ECS tasks,
On-premises servers, the API Gateway,
the SQS queues, [00:00:47 NMADB],
and actually a lot of AWS services.
Also, it is possible for you
within the Step Function workflow
to implement a human approval feature.
For example, a workflow goes up to some points,
and you say, okay, a human will have a look at the results.
And if the human says "Yes," then please go on.
If "No," then fail.
This is something that's possible
thanks to the Step Functions.
So the use cases of Step Functions are manifold,
but, like, we can have, for example, the order fulfillment.
We can have data processing, web applications,

# 216. Amazon Cognito Overview
# Section: Serverless Overviews from a Solution Architect Perspective
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528490
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about Amazon Cognito.
And the goal of it is to give user an identity
to interact with a web and mobile application.
So these users usually sit outside of our AWS account,
hence the name Cognito,
because it gives an identity to users
that we don't know about yet.
So we have two kind of sub-services within Cognito.
We have the Cognito user pool,
and this provides a sign-in functionality
for app users and has really good integration
with API Gateway and the Application Load Balancer.
And we have the Cognito Identity Pool,
used to be called Federated Identity.
And this is to actually provide temporary AWS credentials
to users that are registered with their application
so that they can access some resources of AWS directly.
And there is a good integration
as we'll see with Cognito User Pools.
So if you are asking yourself,
"Don't we already have users in IAM?"
The answer is yes, you do,
but Cognito is gonna be for your web
and mobile application users,
which sits outside of AWS.
So look for the keyword,
such as hundreds of users, or mobile users,
or authentication with whatever mechanism
such as SAML and so on.
So let's do a deep dive into Cognito User Pool or CUP.
So it's a serverless database of users
for your web and mobile application.
And you can define a simple login,
such as username or email and a password as a combination.
You have password reset feature.
You can have email and phone number verification,
multi-factor authentication for users,
and you can also have integration with,
for example, Facebook for your login,
or Google for your login, and so on.
So this Cognito User Pools,
they integrate with the API Gateway
or the Application Load Balancer.
So if we take the example of the API Gateway,
the user is going to connect to your Cognito User Pool,
retrieve a token, pass this token to the API Gateway,
which is going to verify it, and then if it's good,
it's going to translate it into the user identity,
which will be passed to your lambda function as a backend.
And now your lambda function knows
the user it's dealing with,
and the fact that it has a very specific user
that's been really well authenticated.
Alternatively, you can also do the exact same thing
with your Cognito User Pool
on top of your Application Load Balancer.
So that means that your application
will connect again with your Cognito User Pool,
then pass it on to your Application Load Balancer,
and make sure that there is a true login.
And if it's true,
it will redirect the request to your backend,
and pass in some additional headers
with the identity of the user.
So this really allows you
to have in one place either your API Gateway or your ALB,
the certainty that you can verify the login of your user.
So it's a responsibility that you've moved
from your backend to the actual piece
that is going to balance the load for your backend.
So the API Gateway or the ALB.
Okay, the other sub-part of Cognito is
Cognito Identity Pools or Federated Identities.
And it's to get identities for users, but this time,
they don't access our application
through the API Gateway or the Application Load Balancer,
but instead, they're going to directly access
your AWS accounts using temporary AWS credentials.
So the users' source can be, for example,
users that are within Cognito User Pools,
or it can be third party logins,
and then they can access the services
of AWS directly or through the API Gateway.
So the IAM policies applied to the credentials are defined
within the Cognito Identity Pool service already.
And they can be customized
based on the user ID for fine grain control.
And in case you want to have a default IAM role, you can,
so that your guest users or authenticated users
that don't have specific roles defined to them
will inherit this defined IAM role.
So a diagram will surely help you
to understand what identity pools are.
So let's say your web and mobile applications
want to have direct access
into an S3 bucket or DynamoDB table.
So we're going to have Cognito Identity Pools for this.
So the web and mobile application is
going to log in and get a token out of it.
So it could be a login against Cognito User Pools,
or social identity provider,
or SAML, or open ID connect and so on.
And then it's going to take this token
and pass it on to the Cognito Identity Pool service
to exchange this token for temporary AWS credentials.
And to do so,
the Cognito Identity Pool is first going to evaluate
whether or not the token passed is being correct,
meaning the login is valid.
And the second thing it's going to do is
to craft this IAM policy that is specific to that user.
So these credentials now will,
thanks to this very temporary credentials
with associated IAM policy,
will be able to access AWS on your, for example,
your S3 bucket, or your DynamoDB table,
without going through an API Gateway
or an Application Load Balancer.
And this enables for you a use case
where you can do row level security in DynamoDB.
So you would, for example,
have this policy coming out of the Cognito Identity Pools.
And the idea is that in it, you have a condition,
and this condition is saying
that the leading key for DynamoDB
must be equal to the Cognito identity user ID.
And therefore, what's going to happen is
that the user with this policy cannot read
and write all the items in your DynamoDB table,
that would be too much power,
but instead they can only deal with the items
that they have access to through this condition.
So I understand that Cognito is a very complicated service.
Thankfully, you just need to know
at a high level what it means.
So it means that you can create a user base
for your web and mobile application.
It means you can enable row level security in DynamoDB,
for example, to get fine grain access.
And finally, remember this integration
between Cognito User Pools
and your API Gateway or your Application Load Balancer.
Okay, that's it.
I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# 217. Mobile Application: MyTodoList
# Section: Serverless Solution Architecture Discussions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528394
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so let's discuss
serverless architectures now,
and we're going to create
a mobile application called MyTodoList.
So, what we want to do is have the following requirements.
We want to expose a REST API that has HTTPS endpoints.
We want to be serverless architecture,
and we want the users to be able to directly interact
with their own folder in S3
to manage their data if you want to.
And users should be able to also authenticate
through a managed serverless service.
And finally, users can write and read to-dos,
but they mostly read them.
So, maybe there's something to do around performance here.
The database layer should scale
and should have some really high read throughputs.
So, that's a pretty good requirements.
Now, let's see how we can do it.
Number one is to get started, we have mobile clients,
and we talked about doing a REST HTTPS thing.
So, let's use Amazon API Gateway for this.
This is a great way of doing it.
Now, in the classic serverless API fashion,
API Gateway will invoke a Lambda function,
which basically allows us to scale
and use serverless infrastructure.
Okay, Amazon Lambda needs to be able to store
and read to-do from a database.
A database that scales really well
that is serverless is DynamoDB.
So, here we have DynamoDB as our backend.
Now, we said there was going to be also some kind
of authentication layer going on.
So, for this, we can use a serverless technology such
as Amazon Cognito, so our mobile client can connect
and authenticate to Cognito,
and then API Gateway along the way will verify
the authentication with Cognito.
And so, that gives us a very classic serverless API
that we've just created here.
Nothing new for you here, but it's good to see it again.
Now, if you wanna give our users access
to Amazon S3 bucket, how do we do this?
Well, we have our mobile clients
that authenticates to Amazon Cognito
and Cognito that can generate temporary credentials for us
and return these credentials to our mobile clients.
And these credentials allow our mobile clients to store
and retrieve files in Amazon S3
and basically access their own little space in S3.
So, this is a very classic question as well, how to do this?
And the wrong answer is to store
AWS user credentials on your mobile clients.
You definitely do not want to do this.
What you want to do is really use Amazon Cognito,
and then Amazon is free with temporary credentials.
Okay, so it's a very common question.
So, next, our app is starting to scale.
We're starting to get more users,
and it turns out that we, by looking at the patterns,
figure out that we have a very high read throughput.
So, we have many RCUs,
and the to-dos don't really change much.
They don't get edited very often.
So, how can we change this architecture
to basically improve the read throughput
and decrease maybe the cost overall?
What we can do is use DAX as a caching layer.
So, just before DynamoDB, we'll use DynamoDB DAX,
and this will basically have a caching layer.
And because we're doing so many reads,
now the reads will be cached in DAX.
And so DynamoDB, we won't need as much read capacity units.
Maybe we'll scale better, maybe we'll have less cost overall
because so many reads are cached.
And this is a great way overall
to keep on improving our architecture
in a serverless fashion.
Now, there could be another way of doing caching.
Maybe we want to use DAX, but maybe also we want
to start caching the responses
at the Amazon API gateway level.
This is also something we can do,
and this is also a very good one if you think
that the answers never really change
and that you can start caching a few responses
for a few API routes.
So, overall, really interesting to see these kind
of architectures because they really show you
how serverless is done, where the caching appears.
And in this architecture, nothing is managed by us.
We really pay per usage,
and we really don't think about management of databases.
All these things is done by AWS for us.
So, in this lecture,
we've seen the classic serverless REST API architecture,
basically leveraging HTTPS, API Gateway,
Lambda, and DynamoDB.
And then, we've used Cognito
to generate temporary credential, which gives us access
to an S3 bucket with a restricted policy.
And we could use the exact same app pattern using Cognito.
So, our app can access maybe DynamoDB
or Lambda directly or whatever.
This is a very common pattern.
Now, caching the reads on DynamoDB can be done using DAX.
It's a very easy way to enable,
and you can bring not only performance improvement,
but also cost reduction and caching the REST request
can be done at the API Gateway level
if we have very static responses.
Security, finally, for the entire thing can be done
with Cognito and Cognito is directly integrated
with the API Gateway.
So, this was a very basic example,
but it gives us started basically
on serverless architectures
and shows us all the different components we've seen
in the past section.
So, I hope that helps,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 219. MicroServices Architecture
# Section: Serverless Solution Architecture Discussions

Okay, so now we're talking about micro services.
So, not exactly the server-less, but
still a very interesting discussion to have.
So, we want to switch to a micro service architecture
and many services will interact with
each other maybe using a REST API.
So, this is how they have interaction with
one another, they just use the REST API.
Each architecture for each micro service may vary
in form and shape, so we are free to do whatever we want.
And so, we want to use a micro service architecture
for the reason that we want to have leaner
development lifecycle for each service.
We want each service to scale independently
and have it's own quote repository.
So this is why we would use a micro service architecture.
Now, let's have a look, so our users may be able
to talk to our first micro service over HTTPS
and we've decided to have an elastic load balancer
talking to ECS, and then talking to Dynamo DB.
And, it's just a choice we made.
ECS, by the way, if you don't know what it is yet,
it is for docker, so for writing docker containers on AWS.
So that's it, now this micro service
usually has a DNS name or URL, so maybe it's
service1.example.com, and so to get all
that information maybe you will do a DNS Query
to route 53, get an alias record back and then
we can interact with that service.
That's my first service, but maybe we have
a second service, and this one is using
a classic architecture for server-less,
but instead of having Dynamo DB,
we have ElastiCache.
And again, just, you know, something just for fun,
just to mix things up, but we can definitely
use ElastiCache as the back end for Lambda.
So, cool everything works, but maybe
that second micro service, service two,
maybe it also interacts with service one.
So the lambda function will make
a call to our elastic load balancer
because it needs to get some information
from the first micro service to be able to make a response.
And then maybe we have a third micro service,
also using an ELB, but this one
is not server-less, it's using Amazon EC2 auto
scaling and an Amazon RDS database, so more
of the classic architecture we've seen from before.
And it turns out that maybe the EC2 instance
must make a call to the second micro service
before making a decision, so it's represented
here by the dotted lines.
And here, the URL for this is going
to be service3.example.com.
So, it's very simple, but what I
want to show is just have a quick discussion.
You're free to design each micro service
the way you want, and this is why
I had so many different random architectures.
There is two patterns for micro services.
There is a synchronous pattern, so this is
when we make explicit calls to other
micro service, so API Gateway, Load Balancer
are great way to do HTTPS calls to other micro services.
But there is also an asynchronous pattern
that I haven't made into a diagram,
but using SQS, or Kinesis, or SNS,
or Lambda triggers, or S3.
All these things basically we're saying,
"I'm goin to put a message in SQS,
but I don't care when I get a response,
actually I don't care about a response,
something else will happen, though."
And this is an asynchronous pattern.
So, some challenges with micro services,
the first one is that you need to
have some overhead for creating
each new micro service.
And you may get issues optimizing
server density or utilization.
You may get complexity of running
multiple versions of each micro
service simultaneously.
You may get a proliferation of client-side
code requirements to integrate with many
separate services.
But so, most of these challenges,
or some of them, are solved by using
server-less patterns.
For example, API Gateway, Lambda they scale
automatically and then you pay for usage.
So no need to worry about server utilization.
You can easily clone APIs or reproduce
environments in API Gateway.
And you can, for example, generate
client SDK through Swagger integration
for the API Gateway.
So, all in all, what you need to
remember is that micro service is
a design, and you can use any of this for that,
and it does solve some problems,
and it does add some problems.
But at least you get an idea of
how things would work.
Okay, that's it for this lecture.
I will see you in the next lecture.

and it distributes software updates once in a while.

that need to download the patch
and then you download from us and this patch sits on EC2.
So, when a new software update is out,
we are going to get a lot of request
because a lot of people want to update.
And so the content is distributed
in mass over the networking.
It cost us so much money.
Additionally, we really don't want to change
or re-architect our application.
We just wanna optimize our cost and CPU.
Is there an easy way for us to do it?
Of course the answer is yes.
There is.
So, let's talk about the application current state.

running in multi AZ and we'll assume that these M5 instances
are the instances distributing the software updates.

let's say that these software updates
they're put into the Amazon EFS,
so all of them are in the EFS.

How do we basically enable these applications
to scale more globally and to reduce CPU utilization
and to reduce cost.
Super easy.
We just put CloudFront on top of it.
So, CloudFront will be our savior, and why?
Well, there's no changes to architecture.
They will cache software update files at the edge
because the software update files they don't change,
they're not dynamic, there're static,
they're never changing.
And so our EC2 instances, even though they're not serverless
CloudFront is and it will scale for us.
So that means that our ASG will not scale as much
and we'll save tremendously in EC2 class, network class,
EFS class and so much.
And on top of it, we'll save on availability and so on.
So, remember.
CloudFront is such an easy way
to make an existing application more scalable and cheaper
if it's mostly static content just using some caching
at the edges all around the well.
So remember it.
I find it pretty cool.

# 222. RDS
# Section: Databases in AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528402
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Let's do a summary of
what we learned in the Amazon RDS section.
And if you need to go back into any of these points,
I suggest you go back to the old lectures.
This is a summary to summarize what you should know
out of Amazon RDS.
So this is a managed PostgreSQL, MySQL
or Oracle, SQL Server, DB2, MariaDB,
or you have the custom version of RDS.
In Amazon RDS,
you need to provision an RDS instance size,
as well as an EBS volume type and size.
So everything is provisioned,
although you have auto-scaling capability
for the storage layer.
Amazon RDS supports read replicas
to scale read capabilities.
So if you have applications that need to run analytics
against a production database, it is much better
to create a read replica.
And for high availability purposes,
you can use the Multi-AZ to have a standby database,
although that database is just here for
in case a disaster strikes.
You cannot use it
to perform queries against it.
Security for your RDS database is done through IAM,
so you can use, for example,
username and password to connect to your database,
but also you can use IAM authentication,
for some of them.
You have security groups
for network security on your Amazon RDS database,
KMS for at risk encryption,
and you can have intrinsic encryption using SSL and TLS.
Now, if you wanted to do backups,
you have the automated backup option,
which is up to 35 days, and if you use that,
you can do point in time restore to any point
of time in these 35 days,
and this will create a new database out of it,
or if you want to retain backups for longer term recovery,
then you would use a manual database snapshots.
There is a managed
and schedule maintenance,
which will bring downtime into your database.
So this is due to the fact that you have to provision it
and that you have to update.
I mean, AWS has to update at some point database engine
or the underlying EC2 instance
for patches of security and so on.
There is support for IAM authentication on RDS,
and you can enforce it through the RDS proxy,
and it has integration with Secrets Manager
to manage the database credentials.
If you wanted to have access to the underlying instance
and customize it, then you can reuse the RDS custom option
and this is available for the Oracle
and SQL Server type of databases.
So the use cases of Amazon RDS is
to store relational databases.
For example, using the RDBMS
or have an online transaction processing database, so OLTP.
If you wanted to perform SQL queries on top of it
and transactions.
Okay, so hopefully nothing is new for you here.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 223. Aurora
# Section: Databases in AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528406
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's do a summary of Amazon Aurora.
So Aurora is a compatible API for two database engines,
which are PostgreSQL and MySQL.
And Aurora is a very special service
because storage and compute are separate.
So about storage,
while the data is stored in six replicas
across three Availability Zones by default,
and you cannot change this,
therefore Aurora is highly available.
On top of it, in case there is any issue with the storage,
there's going to be a self-healing process
behind the scenes happening.
And if you wanted to increase the storage, no problem.
There is auto-scaling out of the box.
Now, for the compute side,
this is the actual database instances,
they are clustered,
and they can be across multiple Availability Zones
if you wanted to.
And then if you had read replicas,
you could auto-scale them as well
to increase the capacity in case the load increases.
Now, because you have a cluster of database instances,
then you need custom endpoints
to know where to write and read,
and therefore you have a writer endpoint
and a reader endpoint.
You have the same security, monitoring,
and maintenance features as RDS
because, end of the day, they use kind of the same engine.
And you need to know the backup
and restore options for Aurora,
which cannot summarized here,
but I suggest you go back to that lecture
if you ever need to.
Now, some extra features you need to know about Aurora.
The first one is Aurora Serverless.
This is when you have unpredictable
and intermittent workloads,
but you don't need to do any capacity planning,
so it is quite helpful in that use case.
If you wanted to have a global database,
you could use Aurora Global,
and that gives you up to 16 database read instances
in each region where your database is replicated.
And the storage replication happens
in less than one seconds usually across regions,
which is something you have to look out for at the exam.
And in case you have a problem in your primary region,
you can promote a secondary region
to become your new primary.
If you wanted to perform machine learning on top of Aurora,
you could use the Aurora Machine Learning module
to use SageMaker and Comprehend.
If you wanted to use a testing database
or a staging database
out of your production database, for example,
you could use the Aurora Database Cloning feature
to create a new Aurora cluster out of the existing one,
and it is much faster
than doing a snapshot and restoring it.
So the use cases for Aurora are the same as RDS,
but you have less maintenance, more flexibility,
more performance, and more features out of the box,
which makes Aurora a great choice.
Okay, that's it.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 224. ElastiCache
# Section: Databases in AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528412
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So we've learned about
Amazon ElastiCache beforehand,
so let's just do a quick summary.
So ElastiCache is a managed Redis or Memcached for Amazon
so it's a similar offering as RDS,
but this time for caches technology.
So what is a cache?
Well it's an in-memory data store
which gives you sub-millisecond latency
when you want to read data.
So for this, you must provision
an ElastiCache instance type for your cache,
and then you are good to go.
So if you are using Redis, you can have support
for Clustering, Multi AZ, and Read Replicas for sharding,
and you have security provision through IAM.
You can use security groups.
You have KMS at-rest encryption,
and for Redis you have Redis Authentication.
You have the same kind of features as RDS
for backups, snapshots, and point-in-time restore.
You have managed and scheduled maintenance.
And the most important thing
need to remember for the exam
is that if you decide to use Amazon ElastiCache
to perform some caching on top
or combine with an RDS database,
is that to use ElastiCache,
you need to modify your application code
to leverage ElastiCache.
And so if the exam is asking you for a caching solution
that does not require a code change,
then ElastiCache is not a good choice.
Okay?
So the use cases for ElastiCache
are going to be Key/Value store,
when you do frequent read-on-top of your database,
it's good to cache database queries.
Also, if you have session data that needs to be stored
for your users on your website,
ElastiCache is also a very good use case.
And just so you know, you cannot use SQL on ElastiCache.
Okay, that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# 225. DynamoDB
# Section: Databases in AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528408
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's do a summary of Amazon DynamoDB
which appears quite a bit at the exam.
So DynamoDB is a proprietary technology from AWS.
It's a managed serverless
and no SQL database that provides you
out of the box millisecond latency.
You have two capacity modes you need to choose from.
So one of them is the provision capacity
with optional auto scaling, which is great
when you have a smooth type of workload
that increases gradually
over time or decreases gradually over time.
Or you have the on demand capacity mode
where you don't have to provision capacity,
but it scales automatically for you,
which is great if you have very unpredictable workloads
or if you have sudden steep spikes of demand
on your database.
So DynamoDB can replace ElasticCache as a key value store
and it's a great way to, for example, store session data
for your website, combined with a TTL feature
to expire a row after a specific amount of time.
So DynamoDB is highly available.
It is across multiple availability zones by default.
The reads and the writes are fully decoupled
and it's possible for you to have transactions
on top of the DynamoDB tables.
It is possible for you to create a read cache
out of the box that is fully compatible with DynamoDB
which is a DAX cluster, DynamoDB accelerator,
and the particularity of it is
that you get then microsecond read latency.
So look for that in the exam.
In terms of security authentication and authorization,
everything is done through IAM.
You have event processing capability on top of DynamoDB,
so you can enable DynamoDB streams
to stream all the changes happening into your database
and you can have an integration to invoke Lambda
from the DynamoDB stream.
Therefore, Lambda can be invoked
for every single change in your DynamoDB table.
The other option is instead
of standing the data to DynamoDB streams,
you can send the data to Kinesis data streams.
The advantage is that on top of it,
you can use the Kinesis Data Firehose feature,
or you can use any type of integration
that leverages Kinesis data stream.
For example, you could have longer term retention
up to one year on Kinesis data streams.
You have a global table feature on top of the DynamoDB,
which allows you to do active-active replication
across multiple regions.
So anyone can read and write from any region;
this is why it's called active-active.
Now you have two backup options.
The first one is an automated backup.
You need to enable point in time recovery for that
and you can restore your table to a new dynamicDB table
for any point of time up to 35 days.
Or if you want to have longer term retention of backups,
you can enable on-demand backups,
which will also restore to a new table.
Now, you can export your DynamoDB table
to Amazon S3 without using any of the read capacity units
within the Pointing Time recovery windows,
So within 35 days using the export to S3 feature.
And you can also import from S3
without using any right capacity units into a new table.
So DynamoDB, from an exam perspective
anytime you see that you need to rapidly evolve schema
which have a flexible type of database schema
is going to be a great choice.
So the use cases for DynamoDB is when you want a database
and do serverless application development
and your data are small documents, for example,
in the hundreds of kilobytes of size maximum
or when you want a distributed serverless cache.
Okay, so that's it for DynamoDB.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 226. S3
# Section: Databases in AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13672438
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's do a summary
of Amazon S3 from a database perspective.
So S3 is a key-value store for objects,
and it's great when you want to store big objects.
It's not great to store many small objects.
So Amazon S3 is serverless. You have infinite scaling.
The maximum object size is 50 terabytes
and you can version objects over time.
You have different storage tiers.
So you have S3 Standard, Infrequent Access, Intelligent,
and you have Glacier,
and if you want to transition between the tiers,
you can use lifecycle policies.
Some important features need to know about are versioning,
encryption, replication, multifactor authentication deletes,
MFA deletes, and access logs.
In terms of security, you have IAM security,
but you can also have bucket policies
on top of your S3 buckets,
you have ACL, you have access points for Amazon S3,
then you have S3 Object Lambdas
to modify objects before they are sent to the applications,
you have cores, and you have the concept
of object lock or vault lock for Glacier,
which you need to know about in depth.
In terms of encryption mechanisms, we have different ones.
We have SSE-S3, SSE-KMS
where you can bring your own KMS key,
you have SSE-C, you can do client-site encryption,
you have TLS encryption in transit,
and you can set a default encryption scheme
for your S3 buckets.
And if you wanted to operate on all the files
in Amazon S3 buckets at a time,
you can use S3 Batch to do batch operations.
And this is very helpful, for example,
when you want to encrypt unencrypted objects
on an existing Amazon S3 bucket
or when you want to copy existing files
from one bucket to another
before enabling S3 replication.
And to create this list of files,
you can use S3 inventory, for example.
In terms of performance improvements on Amazon S3,
you can use a multi-part upload to upload files
in the parallel way,
you can have S3 Transfer Acceleration
to transfer S3 files faster
from one region to another region,
and S3 Select to only retrieve the data you need
out of Amazon S3.
For automation, you can use S3 Event Notifications.
That has interfaces with SNS, SQS, Lambda, and EventBridge.
And this allows you to, for example, react to events
where new objects are created on your Amazon S3 buckets.
So the use cases for Amazon S3 are around static files.
It's going to be a key-value store for huge files
or website hosting.
So hopefully I'm not teaching you anything new here.
And if you have any doubts on any of these features,
and they can all appear at the exam,
then I would suggest you go back to the Amazon S3 section.
Okay, that's it, I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 228. Neptune
# Section: Databases in AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13672456
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's talk about Amazon Neptune.
Neptune is a fully managed graph database.
So an example of what a graph dataset would be
would be, for example, something we all know,
which is a social network.
So if we look at a social network, people are friends,
they like, they connect, they read, they comment, and so on.
So users have friends, posts will have comments,
comments have likes from users, users share and like posts.
And so all these things are interconnected,
and so they create a graph.
And so this is why Neptune is a great choice of database
when it comes to graph datasets.
So Neptune has replication across 3 AZ,
up to 15 read replicas.
It's used to build and run applications that are gonna be
with highly connected datasets, so like a social network,
and because Neptune is optimized to run queries
that are complex and hard on top of these graph datasets.
You can store up to billions of relations on the database
and query the graph with milliseconds latency.
It's highly available with application
across multiple availability zones,
and it's also great for storing knowledge graphs.
For example, the Wikipedia database is a knowledge graph
because all the Wikipedia articles are interconnected
with each other.
Fraud detection, recommendations engine,
and social networking.
So coming from an exam perspective,
any time you see anything related to graph databases,
think no more than Neptune.
Now Amazon Neptune also has a feature
called Neptune Streams.
So streams in Amazon Neptune are going
to be a real time ordered sequence of data for every change
that happens within your graph data
in your Neptune database.
So that means that whenever an application is writing
to Amazon Neptune,
then the changes will be available immediately
after writing into that Neptune streams.
So in that stream, you have no duplicates
and a strict ordering of changes happening
within your Neptune cluster.
So in a graph, we have rights,
and these rights are written, of course,
to your Neptune cluster, but also to a Neptune stream.
Now this stream data is accessible using an HTTP REST API.
That means that your applications, for example,
that want to read your Neptune Stream,
can use this API to get all the changes in real time.
So the use cases for enabling Neptune streams are,
for example, to send notifications
whenever some changes are made within your graph data,
or to maintain your data synchronized
into another data store.
For example, you want to replicate the changes happening
within your Neptune cluster into Amazon S3 or OpenSearch
or ElastiCache or more.
Or if you want to replicate data across multiple regions
for your Neptune cluster by looking at all the changes
in the stream and rewriting those
into a target Neptune cluster.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 231. Athena
# Section: Data & Analytics
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13672442
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now, let's talk about Amazon Athena.
So Athena is a serverless query service
to help you analyze the data stored in Amazon S3 buckets.
And to analyze this data,
you're going to use the standard SQL language
to query the files.
Behind the scenes,
Athena is built on the Presto engine,
which uses the SQL language.
So the idea is that users are going to load data
into your S3 bucket,
or you are going to load data into your S3 bucket,
and then you would use the Athena service
to query and analyze this data in Amazon S3
without moving it.
So Athena is serverless,
and it analyzes directly your data living in your S3 bucket.
So it supports different formats,
such as CSV, JSON, ORC,
Avro, and Parquet, and possibly others.
And the pricing is very simple.
You're just going to pay a fixed amount
per terabytes of data scanned.
You don't need to provision any database again,
because the whole service is serverless.
So Athena is commonly used with another tool,
called Amazon QuickSight to create reports and dashboards.
So we'll see Quicksight later in depth,
but Amazon Quicksight connects to Athena,
which connects to your S3 buckets.
Now, the use cases for Amazon Athena
are to do ad hoc queries,
business intelligence, analytics, reporting,
and to analyze and query
any kind of logs that originates from your AWS services.
So it could be your VPC flow logs,
your load balancer logs, your CloudTrail trails, and so on.
So as an exam tip,
anytime you need to analyze data in Amazon S3
using a serverless SQL engine,
you can think about Athena.
Now, I've talked about performance improvements,
and you can actually improve Athena performance,
and in this exam,
we'll test you on this as well.
So first of all, because you pay for the amount
of data scanned per terabyte,
you need to use a type of data
where you're going to scan less data.
And for this, you can use a columnar data type
for cost-savings,
because you only scan the columns you need.
So therefore, the recommended formats for Amazon Athena,
are going to be Apache Parquet and ORC,
and it's going to give you a huge performance improvement.
And to get your files into the Apache Parquet or ORC format,
you must use a service
that we'll see as well in this section,
for example, Glue.
Glue can be very helpful
to convert your data as an ETL job,
between, for example, CSV and Parquet.
Now, also because we want to scan less data,
we need to compress data for smaller retrievals.
So there are different compression mechanisms you can use
that have listed it right here.
Next, if you know you're going to query all the time
on some specific columns,
you can partition your datasets,
and partition datasets means that in your S3 bucket,
you're going to have the full path with slashes,
and each slash will be a different column name
with a specific value.
And so you're organizing,
you're partitioning your data in Amazon S3,
so that when you query it,
you can know exactly in which folder
at which path Amazon S3,
you need to scan for data.
So here's an example of data partitions.
So we have flight data in Parquet formats,
and then we do /year=1991.
So we partition by year,
and we'll have one folder for each year.
Then within each year we'll have month,
so month equals one,
and within each month we'll have days,
this equals one.
And so when I do a query on Athena,
and I filter for a specific year,
a specific month, and a specific day,
then we'll know exactly
to which folder in Amazon S3
to get the data from,
and therefore we'll only recover a subset of the data.
Therefore, we'll have really, really good partitioning.
Finally, the last performance improvement you need to do,
is to use bigger files,
it's to minimize your overheads.
So if you have many, many, many small files in Amazon S3,
Athena is not going to be as performance,
as if you had larger files,
for example, 128 megabytes, and over,
because larger files are easier to scan,
and easier to retrieve.
Another feature of Amazon Athena is the Federated Query.
So you know that Athena can query data in S3,
but actually you can query data anywhere,
for example, in relational or non-relational databases,
you can query objects and custom data sources,
would it be on AWS or on-premises.
How? Well, you use what's called a Data Source Connector.
It's a Lambda function,
and that Lambda function is going to run
the Federated Queries in other services.
So that could be, for example, CloudWatch Logs,
DynamoDB, RDS, and so on.
So it's very powerful.
For example, we have Athena here,
and we have a Lambda function,
and you'll have one Lambda function
per Data Source Connector.
And then through Amazon Athena,
you can run the query across ElastiCache,
Document DB, DynamoDB, Redshift, Aurora,
SQL Server, MySQL, HBase on the EMR service,
or any on-premises database.
They're clear from Athena,
as well as, of course, Amazon S3,
and you can do your drawings,
and you can do your competitions, and so on.
That's why it's called a Federated Query.
And then the results of this query
can be stored into your Amazon S3 buckets
for later analysis.
So that's it for Amazon Athena.
As you can see, it's a very powerful service.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.
