# 273. Organizations - Overview
# Section: Identity and Access Management (IAM) - Advanced
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/18078393
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about AWS Organizations.
So it's a global service
and it allows you to manage multiple AWS accounts
at the same time.
So you create an organization
and the main account in your organization
is called the management account,
while the other accounts that join the organization
or that are created from the organizations
are called member accounts.
And remember, accounts can only be part of one organization.
The cool thing about organization
is that the billing is consolidated
across all the accounts.
So you have a single payment method
on the management account
and then it will be paying for all the organization's cost.
But because you have an organization
and it's all part of one big family,
then you get pricing benefits from aggregated usage.
So if you use a lot EC2 or if you use a lot Amazon S3
across all your accounts,
then you will get big discounts,
because it will summarize and sum up
all the usage across all the accounts.
You can also share reserved instances
and saving plans discounts across accounts.
So if a reserved instance is unused in one account,
another account can benefit from it
and therefor the discounts apply
across the entire organization,
which is really good for cost savings.
Now, there's also an API
to automate the account creation
from within the organization.
So you can create accounts very easily
using an organization.
So how does that work?
So we have what's called a root organizational unit, or OU,
and this is the outermost OU of your accounts
and then within it sits the management account.
Then you can create sub-OUs,
so you can create for example an OU for the dev accounts
and then you can create member accounts within the dev OU
or you can create OU for a prod account
and also add member accounts there,
but you can be as free as you want.
You can create within the prod OU,
an OU for your HR member accounts
and an OU for your finance member accounts.
So you can organize it the way you want.
So you have different examples for your OUs.
So you can organize by business units,
so you have for example,
the management account and then the sales,
retail and finance OU
and then different accounts within each OU.
Or you can have an OU by environment,
so for example, one OU for prod,
one OU for test, one OU for dev
and within each OU, some accounts.
Or project-based, so you can have an OU per project
within an account, within each project.
And you can mix and match.
You're really free to do whatever you want.
So what are the advantages of using organizations?
Well, thanks to having multiple accounts,
you can have better security
versus having one account with multiple VPC,
because accounts are more separated than VPCs.
You can also enforce tagging standards
for billing purposes
and you can in one go, enable CloudTrail
for all your accounts
and send all the logs into a central S3 account,
or we can also send CloudWatch logs
to a central logging account
and we can establish cross account roles
for admin purposes automatically.
So we can administer all the other accounts
from the management account.
So these are big advantages.
Also, there's a big security advantage.
We can define service control policies, or SCP,
and it's an IAM policy applied to specific OUs or accounts
and this allows you to restrict
what the users and roles all of them can do
within the accounts.
The SCPs apply to everything
but to the management account,
which will forever have full admin power,
otherwise you could do a mistake
and never come back from it.
So the SCP have the specificity
that if you need to compute what is happening
on this specific account,
you need to make sure that each OU, including the root,
has an explicit allow along the way
to allow a specific action.
This will be very clear in this example.
So let's take for example, a root OU
and we apply full AWS access underneath.
So the management account is under the root OU
and then we have more OU,
the Sandbox, the workload, test and prod,
with accounts within the OUs.
So if we apply an SCP,
which is deny Athena on the management account,
what is happening to the management account?
Well, the management account can do anything,
because there's a role that says that no SCP
ever apply to the management account.
This is a safety, because of course,
if you lock yourself out of your management account,
this would be terrible.
So remember, the management account
can do anything, no matter what.
But let's say for example,
we apply on the Sandbox OU
a full AWS access plus deny S3.
So as you can see, here we still need
to apply full AWS access
to give allow to everything explicitly,
because if we didn't have full AWS access,
then nothing would be allowed within that OU.
So explicit allows are needed every single way.
And on account A, say, we will also do
apply full AWS access and deny EC2,
then account A can do anything,
because it has full AWS access on the root OU
and on the Sandbox OU and on the account itself,
but because we have two explicit denies,
we have one deny S3 from the Sandbox
and one deny EC2 from the account itself,
then it cannot access Amazon S3 or Amazon EC2.
For accounts B and C,
because it don't have a specific SCP attached to them,
then they can do anything except accessing Amazon S3,
because you have an explicit deny
coming from the Sandbox OU.
Next, if we apply full AWS access to the workloads OU
and we also apply an allow EC2 SCP to the test OU
then account D can only access EC2
and if we look at the prod OU
and accounts E and F within it, well, we must first apply
the full AWS access SCP to the prod OU
and then accounts E and F can do anything.
So here are some examples for SCPs.
This is the first one is a blocking of a specific service.
So first, we allow all actions
and then we deny DynamoDB or on the allow list,
here, we allow EC2 and CloudWatch,
but we don't allow anything else.
So those are some examples of SCPs.
So that's it for this lecture, I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 275. Organizations - Tag Policies
# Section: Identity and Access Management (IAM) - Advanced
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/51958341
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about
another kind of policy
you can have on your organization, called a tag policy.
So it looks like this and the idea
is to standardize the tags across the resources
in a specific AWS organization.
So it is used to ensure consistent tagging,
to audit tagged resources,
to maintain proper resources categorization, and so on.
So you define the tag keys and their allowed values,
and then you're going to be able to ascend them directly
to resources or have restrictions on how they're assigned
to resources across all your accounts.
So really to maintain consistency.
Of course, when you want to do cost allocation tags
and attributes-based access control,
this is a great combination
because you restrict what the accounts can do
and so you maintain your consistency across your account,
and so therefore, you can do cost accounting
based on tags and also access control based on tags.
You can also prevent any non-compliant tagging operations
on specified services and resources,
but it doesn't have an effect on resources without tags.
And you can generate a list and a report
that lists all the tagged and non-tagged
or non-compliant resources.
In case you also want to look for non-compliant tags,
you can use EventBridge, okay?
so if you get a question at the exam
around how to maintain tags consistent across accounts,
think about tag policies in AWS organizations.
All right, that's it.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 276. IAM - Advanced Policies
# Section: Identity and Access Management (IAM) - Advanced
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/18078397
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So, now, let's talk about IAM conditions
and what they can imply for your policies.
So, just so you know, they apply to policies within IAM.
So that could be for policies for users,
that could be policies for your resource policies,
for example, for your S3 buckets,
or that could be endpoint policies, and so on.
So, really, anything.
So the first one is aws:SourceIP.
And this is used to restrict the client IP
from which the API calls are being made.
So if we look at this one right here,
it has a Deny star on everything
if it's not an IP address.
And then we have a list of two CIDRs,
of two IP address ranges.
So that means that unless the client makes an API call
from within these IP addresses,
then the API call is being denied.
And this can be used, for example,
to restrict usage on AWS only to, for example,
your company network and, therefore, guaranteeing
that only your company can access your own AWS environment.
So that's one of these conditions.
Then we have aws:RequestedRegion.
So this is, again, something global
because it started at the AWS,
and it's restricting the region the API calls are made to.
So in this one we deny anything on EC2, RDS, and DynamoDB
if we are in the region eu-central-1 or eu-west-1.
Okay, so here we deny access to these services
in the specific regions.
And this can be applied more globally
on their organization SCP to deny or to allow
only access to a specific region.
Next, we have ec2:ResourceTag.
So, as you can see now, the prefix of this tag is EC2,
therefore, this applies to the tags on your EC2 instance.
And, so, here we allow to start and to stop instances, okay,
for any instance if the ResourceTag/Project
is equal to DataAnalytics.
So that means that if the EC2 instance has the correct tags,
being Project and DataAnalytics, then we're good.
But then, as you can see, there is the aws:PrincipalTag,
and this applies to your user tag, okay.
So it's not an EC2 instance tag, this is a user tag.
And, so, your user must also be part
of the department data to perform these actions.
We have aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent
to force multifactor authentication.
So you can have a look at it.
But the user can do anything on EC2,
but they can only stop and terminate instances
if they have MultiFactorAuthenticationPresent,
so this is a deny on the false.
Now let's have a look at an IAM policy for your S3 buckets.
So this is a bucket policy, and we have two statements.
And the first one is a ListBucket,
and this applies to this arn right here, so s3:::test.
Because it's a bucket level permission
and, therefore, we have to specify the bucket itself.
But if we have a look at GetObject, PutObject,
and DeleteObject, this applies to objects within a bucket
and, therefore, your arn is going to be different,
and you're going to have /* to represent
all the objects within your buckets.
And this is why you have a different arn here
because this is an object level permission.
And, again, this is something that can come up in the exam.
Now let's have a look at the resource policies
and the aws:PrincipalOrgID.
So this condition right here, the aws:PrincipalOrgID,
can be used to restrict resource policies
to only accounts that are a member of an AWS organization.
So we have an organization with multiple accounts,
and say we have S3 buckets with this policy on it.
And it's saying that you can do a PutObject or a GetObject
only if the API call is made from an account
that has the PrincipalOrgID of whatever.
And, therefore, it's only going to allow member accounts
from your organization to access the S3 bucket,
but any user outside the organization will be denied
because of this S3 bucket policy.
Okay, so you've seen a lot of different conditions
in now your IAM policies, but hopefully that makes sense,
and it can really start to drill down your use case
and make really advanced use cases in terms of security.
So that's it.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 277. IAM - Resource-based Policies vs IAM Roles
# Section: Identity and Access Management (IAM) - Advanced
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/33878964
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's have a look now
at the fundamental differences
between IAM roles and resource-based policies.
So for cross accounts,
especially when you want to perform an API call
on an S3 bucket cross account,
you have two options.
You can attach a resource-based policy to a resource,
for example, an S3 bucket policy on an S3 bucket,
or you can decide to use a role
that can actually access the resource.
So let's take an example of these two options.
So this is the example
where the user in Account A can assume a role in Account B,
and that role has the permissions
to access your Amazon S3 buckets.
Or similarly, the user in Account A,
through a bucket policy placed on the Amazon S3 bucket
in Account B,
can access the S3 buckets.
So both these two situations are valid,
but there is a little bit of difference, okay?
The first one is an IAM role
that has access to the S3 bucket.
The second one is the S3 bucket policy that allows the user.
So what's the difference?
When you actually assume a role, okay,
you actually give up all your original permissions,
and you take all the permissions assigned to the role.
So this is very important.
That means that we, for example, assume a role,
and this role can do whatever.
We can now do anything that the role does,
but we cannot use our original permissions.
And so when you use a resource-based policy,
instead, the principal does not assume a role,
and therefore, he does not have to give up his permissions.
So if you take an example of user in Account A,
they need to scan a DynamoDB table in Account A,
and then dump it in an S3 bucket in Account B.
What they can do is we should use a resource-based policy
because this way, we don't have to assume a role,
and we can both scan the DynamoDB table
and write to an S3 bucket in another account.
So resource-based policies are supported
by more and more AWS services and resources over time.
So we have the Amazon S3 buckets, the SNS topics,
the SQS queues, the Lambda functions, and so on.
And the big difference of when this comes into play
is when you use Amazon EventBridge.
So when an EventBridge rule runs,
it's going to need permissions on the targets.
And if your target supports resource-based policies,
for example, Lambda functions, SNS topics,
SQS queues, S3 buckets, or API Gateway,
then it's possible that EventBridge
will just add a resource-based policy on the target
to allow the invocation from the EventBridge rule.
That's one case.
On the other hand,
if the resource doesn't necessarily support
a resource policy,
then EventBridge will use an IAM role
to invoke the target service,
for example, for Kinesis Stream, EC2 Auto Scaling,
System Manager Run Command, ECS task, and so on.
And for example, for Kinesis Data Streams,
as a note, it supports resource-based policies,
but still, EventBridge is going to use an IAM role.
So how do you know which one is going to be used in which?
Well, you need to look at the configuration
of the EventBridge role itself
to see how this is going to work,
and then you will know, okay?
But as a matter of fact, Lambda, SNS, SQS,
S3 buckets are using resource-based policies.
And Kinesis Data Streams, EC2 Auto Scaling,
and so on are using IAM roles.
Even though it's possible
for you to use a resource-based policy
with Kinesis Data Stream,
that's not yet supported by EventBridge.
So all the information you need to know
for the exam is on this slide,
and I know that'll be enough for you at the exam.
All right, that's it.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

Let's get into IAM Permission Boundaries.
And so these permission boundaries

And they're an advanced feature

It looks just like an IAM policy.
So we're saying, allow everything on S3 CloudWatch and EC2.
So we attach this, for example, to an IAM user
and that's its permission boundaries.
That means that it can only do things
within S3 CloudWatch and EC2.
And then you need to specify on top of things
an IAM permission through policy.
And so here, say we attach to the very same user,
allow iam:CreateUser, resource *.
So there is a boundary
and there is an IAM policy with permissions.
What is going to be the results permission in this case?
Well, nothing, no permissions
because the IAM policy
is outside the IAM permission boundary.
Therefore, our user is not allowed to create other IAM users
because that is not in its IAM permission boundary.
So I want to show you
where IAM permission boundaries are created.
So let's go create a user.
I'm going to call the user John,
and then I'm going to give him programmatic access.
Next permissions.
I will not set anything,
and next Tags.
Review, and Create user.
So we have created John
and we're going to set permission boundaries for John.
So imagine John is a developer in our company
and he needs to have certain permissions
but we want to make sure that he has a permission boundary.
So for this, we could assign a policy,
for example, for John,
so if I add permission and I say, "Hey, John,
I'm going to attach to you AdministratorAccess."
It seems like John can do everything right now.
So John is a super user.
But I'm also going to set a permission boundary on John.
And I'm going say, okay, here is your boundary
and this is an advanced feature.
And I'm gonna say the only thing you can do, actually,
John, is to have AmazonS3FullAccess.
And so here, what I've been setting
is a permission boundary for John.
And so through this AWS S3 full access managed policy,
even though John has an administrator access,
when John logs in, the only thing he can do is to access S3
because S3 is its boundary.
So here we've seen that,
even though there is a policy attached to John
that gives him an administrator access,
the boundary is actually going to be more restrictive.
So IAM permission boundaries can be used
in combinations of AWS Organizations SCP.
So if look at this diagram,
we have the effective permissions
to be in the middle of your identity-based policy,
so whatever is attached to your user or your group.
The permission boundary, which by the way,
only applies to a user or a role and not a group.
And your organization SCP,
which applies to every single IAM entity in your account.
So in the middle lies what the users can do.
So we can use permission boundaries for a few use cases.
For example, to delegate responsibilities
to non-administrators within their permission boundaries,
for example to create new IAM users.
Or to allow developers to self assign
and manage their own permissions,
while making sure they can't escalate their privileges,
that means making themselves administrators.
Or for example, restrict one very specific user
inside yours organization
instead of applying an entire SCP to your account
and restricting everyone in your whole account.
So let's have a look at the IAM Policy Evaluation Logic.
Because this diagram basically explains to you
how you are authorized, or not, to do actions within AWS.
And you don't need to know by heart,
but it should make sense to you.
So we can see there's a whole flow,
but at every step, there is an evaluation.
And so we're going to look at Deny evaluation,
we're going to look at Organizations SCP,
Resource-based policy,
Identity-based policy,
IAM permission boundaries,
and then finally, Session policies
to allow or deny a specific IAM action.
So let's have a look in details to see how that works.
So we're going to look at all the possible policies in here.
And if there is an explicit deny,
then we know that it's going to be denied automatically.
Then we look at the organizations SCP,
and is there an allow?
If yes, then go to next step.
If not, then it's a deny because it's an implicit deny.
Then we look at resource-based policy,
for example, that can be applied to S3 buckets.
They can be applied to SQS and so on.
And again, we have a look,
is there a resource-based policy?
If so, is there an allow?
Yes or no?
Then we have identity-based policy.
So we look, again, as whether or not
there's an identity-based policy,
whether or not there's an allow,
and then we deny implicitly or go onto the next step.
Then we look at IAM permission boundaries that we just saw.
And then finally, we look at session policies
that won't go over them, this is more related to SDS.
But what I want you to remember is
that all these things are evaluated
when making a specific IAM action.
And so, only if all these things are allowing
and working together, or not denying specifically,
then you will have a final decision allow,
and you'll be able to do your action.
So it's just to give you a bit more overview
but hopefully you understand better
how security works in AWS.
So let's have a look at this policy
and see what it can do to make it a bit more concrete.
So we have sqs:*, Deny on resource *,
and we have action, sqs:DeleteQueue, Allow on resource *.
So first question is,
can you perform sqs:CreateQueue?
The answer is no, you cannot
because there is a Deny star on SQS,
and CreateQueue belongs to that block
and there's a deny on it,
so it's definitely going to be denied.
Now, can you perform an sqs:DeleteQueue?
So there's a deny on the top part
and there's an allow on the bottom part
and they conflict.
There's a deny and allow.
But what did I just tell you?
I told you that as soon as you have an explicit deny,
then the decision is going to be denied.
So because there is an explicit deny on sqs:*,
and sqs:DeleteQueue is within that sqs:*,
then no matter what, even there's an allow here,
this is going to be denied this action.
So you cannot perform sqs:DeleteQueue,
even though you have allowed it explicitly
in the second block.
So very important to know.
And finally, can you perform ec2:DescribeInstances?
So as we can see, there's nothing on EC2 in this thing.
And this is an IAM policy.
And so, because there is no explicit deny
but also there's no explicit allow,
then you cannot perform ec2:DescribeInstances
with this IAM policy.
All right, hope that makes sense.
So that's it for this lecture.
Hopefully you understand IAM better.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# 279. AWS IAM Identity Center
# Section: Identity and Access Management (IAM) - Advanced
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/18078409
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk
about the AWS IAM Identity Center.
And this service is the successor
to something that you used to know probably,
which is called the AWS Single Sign-On Service.
So the idea is that it's the same service,
just been renamed and it gives you one login,
therefore it's called single sign-on,
for all your AWS accounts in the AWS Organizations,
but also your business cloud applications.
So you can connect to Salesforce to Box to Microsoft 365
and so on, or any application you want,
as long as you have a SAML2.0 integration.
And finally, it gives you also a single login
into your EC2 Windows Instances.
So one login, access to everything,
which is really, really good.
And the exam most likely will ask you about one login
into multiple AWS accounts.
Now, the identity provider, so where your users are stored
for this login, can be twofold.
It could be a built-in identity store
in the IAM Identity Center, or you can connect
to a third-party identity provider.
It could be Active Directory, AD,
or OneLogin or Okta and so on.
So just to make it very visible
and visual for you, we have the login flow, such as this.
You go onto the login page, you enter your username
and your password, and then you go directly
into the AWS IAM Identity Center.
And this is actually a screenshot
from my own Identity Center page.
And as you can see from there,
I have enabled it for my AWS accounts.
And so I can click on the account I want
and connect directly, for example,
in the management console.
And then if I do this,
then I'm taken directly from this into the home page
of your console.
But I'm logged in in that specific console.
So the idea is that I don't need to know
how to log in into that specific console.
I can just log in into my IAM Identity Center portal.
And from there I have SSO.
So no need to enter your password once,
it's single sign on,
have SSO access to accounts,
business applications, and so on.
So if in the real world you have multiple AWS accounts,
I would recommend 100% to use this service.
Okay, so now let's talk about how this works.
So the browser interface is going to connect
to the login page of your AWS IAM Identity Center.
And then you have to integrate it, as I said,
with different user stores.
So it could be an Active Directory,
it could be on the cloud or on premises.
And this is where you would use Active Directory
to manage your users and your groups.
Or you can use the IAM Identity Center.
This is the built-in identity store.
And this is where, for example, you would define your users
and your groups as you're used to in IAM.
Then you integrate Identity Center with SSO
for your organization
or your Windows EC2 instances,
your business cloud applications
or your custom SAML2.0-enabled applications.
Again, the cool thing is that you have one login for all
of this, and that simplifies a lot your flow.
Now, of course, when you log in,
you don't have access to everything.
You define something called permission sets
in the Identity Center to define
which users have access to what.
So how does everything relate in IAM Identity Center
for permissions and users and groups?
So we have an organization
and we set up IAM Identity Center
in the management account.
We have two OUs, a development and a production OU,
each with their own accounts.
Now we have two developers in our company.
We have Bob and Alice.
So first of all, we're going to do, just like we do in IAM,
we're going to create a group of developers
for Bob and Alice.
Now we want to make sure that Bob and Alice both have access
to full access of the OU for development.
So we're going to create what's called the permission sets,
and we're going to allow admin access on it.
And then you have to assign this permission set directly
into specific accounts, for example,
your development accounts,
and then you assign this permission set either to your users
or to a group of users, for example, your developers.
So this would allow Bob and Alice to assume a role
with full access on the development account B right now.
You can also have a permission set, for example,
for read-only access
and assign this permission set directly
into your production account,
so account A and account B.
And then you assign this permission set again to Bob
and Alice, which would allow them
to have a read-only access to these accounts.
So now let's talk
about the fine-grained permissions and assignments.
And the first one is multi-account permissions.
So, of course, using the service,
you can manage access across multiple accounts
in your organization.
And using permission sets, you define one
or more IAM policies that you assign to users
and to groups to define what they can access in AWS.
So here is the IAM Identity Center,
and it's integrated with your organization
and you define a permission set for database admins.
So it's a collection of IAM policies.
And you say, for example, that you have access to RDS
and Aurora in your dev account,
as well as RDS and Aurora in the prod account.
And this will automatically create a corresponding IAM role
for your users.
And therefore, when you have your database admins,
it can be a group, for example,
and your users are in this group,
you will assign it the permission sets of database admins.
And whenever users log in through the IAM Identity Center
and access the console of your dev accounts
or your prod accounts,
they will be automatically assuming an IAM role
in that specific account
that will give them the permissions they're supposed
to get, which is pretty good.
So it works the same way.
So you have application assignments
and you can define which users
or groups can access which applications.
And it gives them the required URLs,
the certificates and metadata.
So all of this is supported out of the box.
And something that enables
is called attribute-based access control.
So the idea is that you're going
to have fine-grained permissions
based on the users' attributes stored

So that means that you can have tags and so on.
And using this, you can, for example, assign a user

And the use case of this

# 280. AWS Directory Services
# Section: Identity and Access Management (IAM) - Advanced
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/34466238
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Hey, so now let's talk
about Microsoft Active Directory and AWS Directory Services.
So in case you don't know what Microsoft AD is,
it is a software that is found on
any Windows Server with AD Domain Services.
And it's a database of objects,
and the objects can be user accounts, computers, printers,
file shares, security groups.
So all your users manage
within your entire Microsoft ecosystem on premise
is going to be managed by Microsoft Active Directory.
And there's going to be a centralized security management.
You can create account, assign permissions, and so on.
And all the objects will be organized into a tree.
And a group of tree is called a forest.
That's just for some terminology.
So let's take an example, we have a domain controller
and we're going to create an account on it.
We're create an account username is John,
and the password is Password.
And the idea is that
all the other Windows machines we have within our network
are going to be connected to the domain controller.
So that's if we're using the John password
on the first machine,
it's going to look it up in the controller and say,
yes, we have that login.
And then, allow you to log in from that machine.
So all these machines are going to be connected
to your domain controller and that allows you
to have the users accessible on any single machine.
So that's the whole idea behind Active Directory
in a very, very high level.
Now we have AWS Directory Services,
which is to provide you
a way to create an Active Directory on AWS.
And we have three flavors on it.
We don't have to do a deep dive on them,
but you have to understand the differences
between these three flavors.
The first one is AWS Manage Microsoft AD
to create your own Active Directory in AWS.
And you can manage users locally
and it supports multi-factor authentication.
The idea is that with this standalone Active Directory,
you can also create a trust connection
with your on-premise AD
where you have your own users there as well.
And what that means is that your AD in here, for example,
can be trusted with the on-premise AD.
So AWS trust the on-premise AD
and on-premise AD trust AWS.
And so that means that if your users
authenticated to the right,
and used an account that is not managed by AWS,
it can go and look up the accounts
into the on-premise Active Directory.
And similarly, if an on-premise directory user goes
and authentic to your on-premise AD using the AWS accounts,
it can be trusted to go and look it up.
So here our users are going to be shared
between our on-premise Active Directory and AWS, okay?
A little bit complicated, I know if you're new to this,
but hopefully it makes sense.
The AD Connector is a little bit different.
This is a direct gateway proxy to redirect to on-premise AD
and it supports MFA if you need multi-factor authentication
and the users are solely managed into the on-premise AD.
So here is the example.
In this example, our AD Connector is just acting as a proxy.
So if the users try to authenticate with our AD Connector
it's going to proxy the request
back to our on-premise AD and look it up.
So the idea here is that
in the first case with Microsoft Managed Microsoft AD,
we have users sitting in AWS Managed AD
and users sitting in on-premise AD.
Whereas with Ad Connector, as the name indicates,
it connects, it proxies
the queries, the connection requests
back to our on-premise Active Directory.
And the only place where we can manage users
is going to be on the on-premise AD.
Finally, you have Simple AD.
And it's an AD-compatible managed directory on AWS.
It doesn't use Microsoft Directory.
And it cannot be joined with a non-premise Active Directory.
So the idea is that if you don't have an on-premise AD
and you need an Active Directory for your AWS Cloud,
then you can have just a Simple AD as a standalone thing.
And the idea here is that using Active Directory
you can create EC2 instances
that are going to be running Windows.
And these Windows instances can join the domain controllers
for your network
and share all the logins, and the credentials, and so on.
So this is why we want to have a directory in AWS
to have a directory closer
to your EC2 instances running Windows.
And hopefully that makes sense.
Now, the exam should has queue
some very, very high level question,
saying we want to proxy our users to on-premise
and therefore you need AD Connector,
or we want to manage our users
on the cloud in AWS and have MFA
and therefore you need AWS Managed AD,
or we just want a Simple AD
and we don't have any on-premise stuff.
In this case, you want a Simple AD.
So now something that you know
is how to integrate the IAM Identity Center
with Active Directory.
So if you connect to an Active Directory
that is managed on your AWS using the directory service
then the integration is out of the box.
You just tell IAM Identity Center
to integrate and connect to your AWS Managed Microsoft AD.
Very simple.
But what if you don't manage
your Active Directory users on the cloud?
What if you have a self-managed directory
for example, on premises?
In that case, you have two ways of connecting
to your self-managed directory.
The first one is what we should call
a two-way trust relationship
using the AWS Managed Microsoft AD.
So you would create a Managed Microsoft AD
from the directory service,
and then you would set up a two-way trust relationship
between your Active Directory,
for example on premises and your Managed AD.
And then you would use the out of the box integration
coming from the IAM Identity Center for single sign-up.
The other option would be to use an AD Connector.
So an AD Connector here would have the role
to of course integrate with IAM Identity Center.
And then you would connect to it
and then it would automatically proxy any kind of request
onto your self-managed directory.
So if you had to choose one or the other,
it will depends on
if you want to also be able to manage users
from within the cloud on Active Directory in the cloud.
And then the first solution may better.
But if you just wanted to proxy API calls
then the second solution could be a fit,
although with a bit more latency.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 282. AWS Control Tower
# Section: Identity and Access Management (IAM) - Advanced
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/34465994
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk
about the AWS Control Tower service.
So it's a very easy way for you to set up and govern
a secure and compliant multi-account AWS environment
based on best practices.
So actually to create these accounts,
well, the Control Tower service
is going to use the AWS Organization service
and then the accounts are automatically being created
and we'll see in the next slide
how to make them secure and compliant.
And so the benefits of using a Control Tower
is that you automate the set up
of your environments in a few clicks
and you have all your configs you want in advance.
Then you can automate
ongoing policy management using guardrails.
I will show you this in the next slide.
You can detect policy violations
and remediate them automatically,
and you can monitor the overall compliance
of all your accounts through an interactive dashboard.
So it's yet another service on top of organizations.
So what are these guardrails?
So say you set up multiple accounts on AWS,
but you want to restrict all of them at once
for certain kind of things,
or you want to monitor the compliance
for certain kind of things.
So using these guardrails,
you're going to get ongoing governance for all your accounts
within your Control Tower environments.
So you have two kinds of guardrails.
The first one is called a preventive guardrail.
And so it's to prevent accounts from doing something
and therefore they're restrictive.
And so we're going to use SCP, so Service Control Policies,
from the AWS Organization service
to apply them to all our accounts.
For example, we could create a preventive guardrail
to restrict regions across all your accounts to say,
hey, you should only operate in the us-east-1
in the eu-west-2 regions.
And so therefore behind the scenes,
Control Tower is going to tell organizations to use SCPs.
The second kind of guardrail we have
is a detective guardrail.
So this time, we want to just detect non-compliance.
And because I talk to you about compliance,
of course, it's using the AWS Config service.
For example, we want to identify untagged resources
in our accounts.
So we have Control Tower
and we set up a detective guardrail.
And so it's going to use Config
and Config is going to be deployed
on all your member accounts
and is going through the rules,
monitor any untagged resources.
In case anything is non-compliant,
it's going to trigger an SNS topic.
So we could be notified as an administrator
or the SNS topic can also invoke a Lambda function.
And the Lambda function
can automatically remediate the action
and add tags to your untagged resources.

# 284. Encryption 101
# Section: AWS Security & Encryption: KMS, SSM Parameter Store, Shield, WAF
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528512
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so in this lecture,
if you're not too familiar with how encryption works,
I want to give you a little bit of details
on how it works at a high level.
So, first let's talk about encryption in flight,
which is going to be referred as TLS or SSL.
TLS is the newest version of SSL.
So what we have is that the data is going to be encrypted
before sending the data.
And then it will be decrypted after receiving it.
So this is for communication
between a client and a server over a network.
And so what's going to be happening
is that for encrypting the data
TLS certificates are going to be used.
And this is what you see when you go onto websites
and it says HTTPS, that means that the connection
between you and the server
is going to be encrypted using TLS certificates.
Why do we want encryption in flight?
Well, because we're sending data over a network
and sometimes a public network
and the data goes around many different servers.
We don't want to be having a man in the middle attacks
where a middle server receives the data
and just observes the packages we're sending to the server.
And so what we want to have HTTPS or TLS, or SSL,
this is when we know that only the target server
can decrypt the encrypted data we're sending.
So let's take an example.
We have a client and a server
and we want to be able to securely login
into the server by providing our username and password.
But we only want the target server to be able to receive it.
So we're going to have the username and password
and then we're going to apply TLS encryption
on the client side automatically.
The data is going to be encrypted and sent over the network.
So as you can see, no between server can decrypt the data
and only the target server
can use the TLS decryption mechanism
to decrypt that package
and then see that we've sent the username and password.
And therefore say that we're securely logged in.
So that's for encryption in flight.
The next one is around the server side encryption at rest.
The idea is that the data will be encrypted
after being received by the server
so that it's stored securely.
And then it will be decrypted
before being sent back to our clients.
It will be stored in an encrypted form
thanks to a key, and that key is usually a data key.
And so the whole idea of managing these keys
for encryption and decryption
is that the management must happen somewhere
and the server must have access to these keys.
So let's take a service,
for example, Amazon S3.
We're sending an object over HTTP,
maybe even HTTPS for inflight encryption.
And so the service receives our object, but it is decrypted.
So the service can use a data key,
and using the data key and the decrypted objects,
we can have encryption of that object at rest.
And then when it comes to sending back that object
to the clients, the encrypted objects and the data key
will be used together to decrypt.
We'll have a decrypted form of object,
and then that object will be sent over HTTPS
back to the clients.
So we received the decrypted object as is.
As we can see in this case,
there is a server side encryption
because all the encryption and decryption
happens on the server.
So finally let's talk about client-side encryption.
And the idea is that this time
the data is encrypted and decrypted at the client side.
And the server should never be able to decrypt the data
because we don't trust a server in that case.
So for this, we could leverage encryption
for this mechanism.
So let's have an example.
The client has an object
and the data key this time is client side.
And after encryption, we get an encrypted object.
That encrypted object can be sent then securely
to any storage service available, an FTP server,
Amazon S3, EBS volumes, et cetera.
And they will be stored in encrypted form.
So the entire server can not even decrypt the data contents.
When we retrieve the contents,
we retrieve the encrypted object directly.
And if we still have access to the data key client-site,
then we're able to perform the decryption mechanism
and get the decrypted objects back.
So that's it for the three encryption mechanisms
we can see in the Cloud.
I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# 285. KMS Overview
# Section: AWS Security & Encryption: KMS, SSM Parameter Store, Shield, WAF
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528514
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about AWS KMS,
which is a key management service of AWS.
So we've been using it a lot without knowing,
but anytime you hear encryption
when you have an AWS service,
it's most likely going to be KMS encryption.
The aim is that with this KMS service,
AWS is going to manage the encryption keys for us.
And that's great,
because that means that we have less things to do.
So KMS is, of course,
fully integrated with IAM for authorization,
and it gives us very easy ways to control access
to our data if it's encrypted with KMS.
The power of using AWS KMS is that you're able
to audit every single API call made to use your keys
through CloudTrail,
which is something the exam may test you on.
So on top of it,
KMS can be used seamlessly into most AWS services.
So for example, if you wanted to encrypt the data at rest
in an EBS volume, just enable the KMS integration.
Same for S3, same for RDS, same for SSM,
and same for pretty much all the services
that require encryption.
The idea is that with KMS, you can also use it yourself.
And if you have secrets data,
you never ever store them in plain text,
that means just as is.
Especially in your code.
So if you want to use KMS,
you can also use KMS through API calls.
You can use the AWS CLI or the SDK.
And that means that you can encrypt
whatever is a secret for you with a KMS key.
And then these encrypted secrets can be, for example,
stored in your code or in environment variables.
That is a much better pattern.
So now let's talk about the different types
of KMS keys available to you.
So now it's called a KMS key.
By the way, it used to be called
the KMS customer master key, but it was confusing
because there's also the customer managed keys
as we'll see in a second.
So now, we just talk about KMS keys.
So we have two types of KMS keys.
We have the symmetric KMS keys,
and that means there's only one single encrypted key
that is used to encrypt and decrypt data.
And so any service of AWS that is integrated
with KMS will use symmetric keys.
The idea is that when we create or use a KMS symmetric key,
then we never get access to the key itself, okay?
All we do is that we use the KMS API calls
to leverage and use that key.
The second kind of key available on KMS
are called asymmetric keys.
That means that you have two keys.
You have a public key that's used to encrypt data,
and a private key used to decrypt data.
So this is used when you have encrypt/decrypt,
or sign/verify type of operations.
And in that case,
you can download the public key out of KMS,
but you can use access the private key.
You can only use API calls
against to access the private key.
So the use cases for an asymmetric type of key
is when you want the encryption to be done outside
of your AWS cloud by users who cannot
or don't have access to the KMS API key.
In which case they will use the public key
to encrypt the data.
Send it over to you.
And you within your account,
you would use the private key of AWS to decrypt that data.
So within the world of KMS keys,
you have different types of KMS keys.
The first one are AWS owned keys.
They're free, and this is the kind of key you would use
when you use SSE-S3 type of encryption,
or SSC DynamoDB, where you have the option, for example,
that you choose a key owned by DynamoDB.
So these are not really KMS
because you don't really see them,
but they're types of encryption keys within AWS.
Then you have the AWS managed keys, and they're free,
and you will recognize them
because they start with AWS slash and then the service name.
For example, AWS/RDS or AWS/EBS,
or in this example, AWS/DynamoDB.
They're free and you can just use them as you please,
but only from within the service that it's assigned to.
Then you have your own customer managed keys
and their custom keys, and they cost you $1 per month.
And if you want to import them as well, you can import them,
and they cost you $1 per month.
KMS also has a pricing where you're going to pay
for each API call made to the KMS service,
which is about 3 cents per 10,000 API calls.
You also have automatic key rotation.
So if it's an AWS managed KMS key,
then it's automatic every one year.
And if it's a customer managed key,
you can enable automatic rotation and you set the period,
and you can also have on-demand rotation of your key.
And if it's imported KMS key,
then you can only manually rotate it.
And for this, you need to leverage an alias.
So KMS keys are scoped per region.
That means that if you have an EBS volume encrypted
with KMS key in a region, for example, EUS2,
then if you want to copy that to a different region,
we have to do several steps.
First of all, we have to take a snapshot of this EBS volume.
And if we take a snapshot from an encrypted snapshot,
then this snapshot itself will also be encrypted
with the same KMS key.
Then to copy the snapshot to another region,
we need to re-encrypt the snapshot using
a different KMS key.
And this is something AWS will do for you.
But the same KMS key cannot live in two regions.
So now we have an EBS snapshot,
it's encrypted with KMS with a different key,
and it lives in another region.
Now, we restore the snapshot
into its own EBS volume with KMS,
and it's KMS key B into the region AP southeast two.
Now, the other thing we need
to know about is KMS key policies.
So this is to control access to your KMS keys.
It's similar to an S3 bucket policy.
With a difference that if you don't have the KMS key policy
on your KMS key, then no one can access it.
So in that regards, we have two types of KMS key policies.
We have the default one,
and it's created if you don't provide
a specific custom KMS key policy.
And the idea is that the default allows
everyone in your account to access this key.
That means that if you have an IAM policy allowing a user
or role to access this key policy, you're good.
But if you want to have more specific controls over it,
you could use a KMS key policy that is custom.
In which you define the users,
the roles that can access your KMS key.
And you define who can administer the key.
And this is especially helpful
if you want to do cross account access for your KMS key,
because we can authorize another account to use our KMS key.
So when do we use this?
Well, for example,
if we wanted to copy an encrypted snapshots across accounts.
So we create a snapshot encrypted with our own KMS key,
and it's a customer managed key.
It must be that because we need
to attach a custom key policy.
And then we attach a KMS key policy
to authorize for cross account access.
It looks like this.
Then we share the encrypted snapshot
with the target account.
And then in the target account,
we create a copy of the snapshot
and we encrypt it with a different customer managed key
in that target account.
And then we can create a volume from the snapshot
in the target account, and we're done.
So that's a lot of information by KMS,
but let's go into hands-on
to hopefully learn a bit more about it.

# 287. KMS - Multi-Region Keys
# Section: AWS Security & Encryption: KMS, SSM Parameter Store, Shield, WAF
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/33878976
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So, now let's talk about KMS Multi-Region keys.
So, we have KMS and we can actually have a Multi-Region key.
That means that you're going to have your primary key
in one selected Region, such as for example, us-east-1.
And then, that key is going to be replicated
to other Regions.
For example, us-west-2, eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-2.
And so the similarity is that
the key material is going to be replicated.
The same key is going to be in other Regions.
And the key ID is going to be the exact same.
So as you can see the key ID slash mrk and then whatever
is the same across all Regions.
And this is the principle behind the KMS Multi-Region keys.
So, what would you use them?
Well, it's a set of KMS keys
that you can use in different AWS Regions
and they can be used interchangeably.
So that means that you can encrypt in one Region
and then decrypt in another Region.
And Multi-Region keys they're possible
because they have the same key ID, the same key material.
And if you have automatic rotation enabled
for the primary key, and it actually rotates
it's going to be also replicated to the other Regions.
So the idea with that, with the Multi-Region key,
you can encrypt in one Region and decrypt
in another Region, and you don't need therefore
to re-encrypt your data
when moving from one Region to the next;
or to make cross Region API calls.
So something to understand though
is that KMS Multi-Region keys are not global.
Okay? You have your Primary and your Replicas.
And each Multi-Region key
is going to be managed independently
with its own key policy and so on.
So it's not recommended to use Multi-Region key,
except in very specific use cases
because KMS likes to have the fact that
a key is bounded to a single Region.
And so the use cases for using Multi-Region keys
is if you want to have a global client-side encryption.
So to be able to encrypt client-side in one Region
and to decrypt client-side in another Region.
or to do encryption on Global DynamoDB tables
or on Global Aurora.
And we'll see this in a second.
So how does it work when you use
Global Tables in DynamoDB and KMS Multi-Region key
with client side encryption?
So the idea is that you want to encrypt
not just the whole table
because this is just at risk encryption.
You want to encrypt actual attributes on your table.
And so that they're only available to specific clients.
Not even to database administrators.
For this we're going to use
the Amazon DynamoDB Encryption Clients.
So let's take an example where we have us-east-1
and ap-southeast-2.
So the KMS service is having a Multi-Region key
which is replicated to another Region.
The Region ap-southeast-2.
And the client application wants to insert data
into a DynamoDB table.
So first is going to encrypt the attribute
that it needs to be encrypted
with the primary Multi-Region key.
So the idea is that the DynamoDB table,
most of the fields will not be encrypted client-side. Okay.
But then one of them, for example
the Social Security number is going to be encrypted.
So this is great because well,
your database administrators
that have accessed your DynamoDB table,
if they don't have access to the KMS key
that we used to encrypt that one attribute,
the Social Security number.
Then they will not be able to access it.
So it gives you a protection even
against the database administrators.
So if this DynamoDB table happens to be a Global Table
then this data is going to be replicated to another Region.
And so this is now in ap-southeast-2.
And thankfully we've decided to encrypt our data,
the attributes, with a Multi-Region key.
And therefore, a client's application
in the ap-southeast-2 Region can retrieve the row,
see that one attribute is encrypted
and then perform an API call
to actually decrypt the attribute
with the replica Multi-Region key.
And this is why we are doing Multi-Region key this instance.
Is it so that client applications in the ap-southeast-2
can do a local API call to KMS
to decrypt that one attribute.
So using this client-side encryption technique
we can protect specific fields or attributes on our data
and only guarantee decryption when our client has access
to an API key.
And thanks to Global Tables
we can make sure the data and the encryption keys
are also replicated together.
So the same concept can be applied to Global Aurora.
So I will go a bit faster.
And this time we're going to use the AWS Encryption SDK.
So we have two Regions
and we have a Multi-Region key in KMS
replicated across these two Regions.

with a table.
And so all the data is unencrypted on this one row,

Now this is a Global Database.
So that means that the tables are going to be

And therefore the same data is going to happen to be

And because we have clients in the ap-southeast-2

So if you enable S3 Replication from one bucket to another,
then any unencrypted objects
and objects encrypted with SSE-S3
will be replicated by default.
Objects that are also encrypted with SSE-C,
with the customer provided key,
can also be replicated,
and then we have objects encrypted with SSE-KMS.
So by default, they're not replicated
but we need to enable the option
to actually replicate these objects.
And so we specify with which KMS Key
we want to encrypt the objects within the target buckets,
and then we adapt this KMS Key Policy for the target key
and we create an IAM Role
that is allowing the S3 Replication service
to first decrypt the data in the source bucket
and then re-encrypt the data in the target bucket
with the target KMS Key.
And so when you do so, this enables replication
because there is a lot of encryption
and decryption happening.
You may get KMS throttling errors,
in which case you need to ask for a service quotas.
So the question you may have is
should I use multi-region key with S3 Replication?
And the documentation says that you can use multi-region key
for S3 Replication
but currently they are treated as independent keys
by the Amazon S3 service,
and therefore the object is still going to be decrypted
and then encrypted using the same key
even though the key is a multi-region key, okay?
So this is it for this lecture,
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 289. Encrypted AMI Sharing Process
# Section: AWS Security & Encryption: KMS, SSM Parameter Store, Shield, WAF
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/33879006
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So here is a question that can come up
in the exam.
This is around the process to share an AMI
with another account, and the AMI has been encrypted
with a KMS key.
So the AMI is in your source account,
and it's encrypted with your KMS key.
So how do you launch an EC2 instance
in account B from the AMI in account A?
So first you must modify the AMI property
with a launch permission, and the list launch permission
allows account B to launch this AMI.
So effectively, this is how you share an AMI.
You must modify the launch permissions
and add the specified target to its account ID.
Then you need to also share the KMS key
for the accounts B to be able to use it.
So this is done usually with a key policy.
Then in account B, you would create an IAM role
or IAM user with enough permissions to actually
use both the KMS key and the AMI.
So you must have it on the KMS side, access to the
Describekey API call, the ReEncrypted API call,
CreateGrant and Decrypt API calls.
And then once all of this is done, you can simply launch
an EC2 instance from that AMI and optionally
the target accounts can choose to re-encrypt everything
with the KMS key that it's owned, that it owns
in its own accounts, to re-encrypt the volumes.
But there you go, you can launch an EC2 instance.
And so if you understand this process you're good to go
to maybe answer one question at the exam.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 290. SSM Parameter Store Overview
# Section: AWS Security & Encryption: KMS, SSM Parameter Store, Shield, WAF
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528518
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about
the SSM Parameter Store.
It's a secure storage for your configuration
and your secrets.
And optionally,
you can choose to encrypt these configurations
and therefore make it secrets
by using the KMS service.
SSM Parameter Store is serverless,
it's scalable, it's durable,
and the SDK is very easy to use.
On top of it, if you update your parameters
then you have version tracking of them.
The security is provided through IAM
and you get notifications with Amazon EventBridge,
in certain amount of cases.
You have full integration with CloudFormation.
That means that CloudFormation can leverage the parameters
from parameter store as input parameters for your stacks.
So let's take an example.
We have an application
and then we have the SSM parameter store.
So we can store plain text configuration in this way.
Then the IAM permissions of your applications
are going to be checked.
For example, your EC2 instance role
or you can have encrypted configuration.
In that case
the SSM parameter store is going to encrypt it with KMS.
And so the KMS service is going to be used
for encryption and decryption.
And of course, you need to make sure
that your applications do have access
to the underlying KMS key to perform that encryption
and that decryption.
So you can store parameters in the parameter store
with a hierarchy.
So for example, you can define my department
as a path and underneath the My-app and then the Dev
and then we have the Dev DB-URL
and then the DB-password within that folder.
So that means that your parameters goes all the way down
into the hierarchy.
We can go one level up and store a parameter
for the Prod DB-URL, as well as a Prod DB password
and go up to another app or another department.
That really allows you to organize your parameters
the way you want in a structured fashion.
And then this is going to simplify your IAM policies to
allow applications to have access to an entire department,
or to an entire app,
or just to an app department environment specific path.
You also have the opportunity
to access Secrets of Secrets Manager
through the Parameter Store
by using this reference right here.
So it's a little trick that not many people know.
And there are something called Public Parameters
that are issued by AWS that you can use.
For example, if you want to find the latest AMI
for the Amazon Index 2 in your specific region.
This is something that's available
within the Parameter Store as an API call.
So if you take an application,
for example our Dev Lambda function is going to have
an IAM roll that allows it to access
the DB-URL and DB-password within the Dev of my app.
And then if you have a Prod Lambda Function,
thanks to again, a different IAM policy
and maybe some environment variables,
you can access the Prod DB-URL
and Prod DB-password of another path.
(mouse clicks)
Now, within Systems Manager,
you have two kinds of parameter tiers.
You have the standard and the advanced tier.
So the big difference is going to be around the size
of 4KB which is 8KB,
and also the availability of a parameter policy.
For the standard one, we have none but for advanced,
we have some.
The advanced type of parameters
is going to be a $0.05 per month.
Whereas the first one is going to be free.
So what are these parameter policies?
And this is only for advanced parameters.
(mouse clicks)
Well, this allows you to assign a time to live
to a parameter, that means an expiration date.
So that you forced users to update
or delete sensitive data such as passwords.
And you can assign multiple policies at a time.
So here is an example policy.
So this is an expiration policy to delete a parameter
and you say, "Hey, on this time stamp
you must delete these parameter."
And then through the EventBridge integration,
EventBridge is going to get notifications of it.
So in this example, 15 days before the parameter expires
we'll receive notification in EventBridge
which gives us enough time to actually update it
and make sure the parameter is not getting deleted
because of the TTL.
Or maybe sometimes you wanna make sure the parameters
change once in a while.
So you can have a no change notification in EventBridge
so that if a parameter has not been updated for 20 days,
then you will be notified as well.
So you can get very, you know,
creative with the parameter store.
But now you get the idea behind it.
So I hope you like this lecture
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# Section: AWS Security & Encryption: KMS, SSM Parameter Store, Shield, WAF

So now let's talk about a very simple service
called the AWS Secrets Manager.
So it's a newer service and it's meant for storing secrets
and it's going to be different from the SSM parameter store,
because on Secrets Manager, you have the capability to force
the rotation of secrets every X number of days,
and therefore you have a better secret management schedule.
On top of it, from within Secrets Manager,
you can force and automate the generation
of secrets on the rotation.
And for this, you have to define a Lambda function
that will generate that new secrets.
Moreover, Secrets Manager is really well integrated
with different services on AWS.
And I just showed you Amazon RDS
for example, for MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL or Aurora.
But there are other services as well with AWS,
other databases, that are integrated
with Secrets Manager out of the box.
That means that the username and the password to get into
your database is stored directly in Secrets Manager
and it can be rotated and so on.
Now, Secrets can be encrypted using the KMS service.
And so anytime in the exam you see Secrets,
or integration for RDS,
or for Aurora of Secrets, really think Secrets Manager.
There's one more feature we need to know about
which is the concept of multi-region Secrets.
So the idea is that you can replicate your Secrets
across multiple AWS regions
and Secrets Manager Service will keep readers
in sync with the primary Secrets.
So here have two regions.
We create a Secret in the primary one
and it gets replicated as a same Secret
into a secondary region.
Now, why would we do this?
Well, multiple things.
Number one, in case there is a problem with US East 1,
you're able, for example, to promote a replica Secret
as a standalone secret.
And then thanks to the fact that that Secret is replicated
across regions, then you can build multiple regions apps.
You can also have disaster recovery strategies,
or if you have an RDS database that is also being replicated
from one region to the next,
then you can use the same Secret to access,
the same, the RDS database, the corresponding one,
in the corresponding region.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 294. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
# Section: AWS Security & Encryption: KMS, SSM Parameter Store, Shield, WAF
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/33879018
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about the AWS
Certificate Manager Service, also called ACM.
So with ACM, you can easily provision, manage,
and deploy TLS certificates on AWS.
What are TLS certificates used for?
And they sometimes say SSL.
So they're used to provide
in-flight encryptions for websites.
You know when you go to websites,
and it says HTTPS, the S stands for secure,
and therefore this is where you know
that there is a TLS certificate involved in the transaction.
So how does that work?
Well, you have an ALB, for example,
connected to your Auto Scaling group,
but you want to expose your application load balancer
as an HTTPS endpoint.
Therefore, you would integrate it with a certificate manager
to provision and maintain TLS certificates
directly on your application load balancer,
and your users will access your websites
or your API using the HTTPS protocol.
So ACM supports both public and private TLS certificates
and is free of charge
if you want to use public TLS certificates.
There is also a feature
to automatically renew these certificates,
we will see this in a second on other slides,
and you have integrations with many AWS services,
so you can load TLS certificates on elastic load balancers,
for example, the classic one, the application load balancer
or the network load balancer,
CloudFront distributions,
or any APIs on the API Gateway.
So what's the process to request a public certificate?
First of all, you need to list the domain names
that are going to be included in your certificates.
So they could be a fully qualified domain name, FQDN,
such as corp.example.com,
or it could be a wildcard domain,
for example, *.example.com,
and you can include as many domains as you want.
Then you select the validation method.
Would it be through DNS validation
or through email validation?
And for automation purposes,
when it comes to automatically renewing
your SSL certificates,
DNS validation is going to be a preferred method.
And for email validation,
what's going to happen is that ACM
is going to send emails to contact addresses
in the registrar for your domain
and verify that you did request that certificates.
And if you decide to do DNS validation,
then you will have to create a CNAME record
in your DNS configuration
to verify that you own the domain.
And so, if you have Route 53, for example,
then it's automatically integrated with ACM
to do this for you.
Next, you have to wait a few hours to get verified
and then your certificate will be issued,
and this public certificate
will also be enrolled for automatic renewal,
that means that automatically
ACM will renew any ACM-generated certificates
60 days before expiry,
which gives you a lot of peace of mind.
So when it comes to ACM,
what if you import a public certificate?
So you have the option
to actually generate a certificate outside of ACM
and then import it into ACM.
But, in that case,
because it's been generated outside of ACM,
there is no automatic renewal.
And so therefore,
before your existing certificate expires,
you need to import a new one.
And how do you know when a certificate is going to expire?
Well, the ACM service is going to send
daily expiration events starting 45 days prior to expiration
into your EventBridge service.
And the number of days can be configured.
You can set 45, you can say 30, whatever you want.
So that means that daily, you will have an event,
in EventBridge for expiring certificates,
and that's one way of doing it.
And then from EventBridge,
then you can trigger Lambda functions
or SNS topics or SQS queues.
There's another way to use AWS Config,
and there is a managed rule in Config
called the ACM Certificate Expiration Check,
and it's going to check for expiring certificates.
You can configure the number of days again.
And so the Config service
is going to have a rule that will check the ACM service,
and then if any certificate is deemed not compliant,
then the event of non-compliance
will be sent to EventBridge.
And yet again, we can trigger Lambda, SNS, or SQS.
So two ways of getting these automatic alerts.
Now, how does the ACM service integrate with ALB?
So we've seen kind of an ALB
with an Auto Scaling group in the backend,
and we can provision and maintain a TLS certificate
through the ACM service.
But there is a very good specificity.
On your ALB,
you can set a redirect rule from HTP to HTTPS.
That means that if your user is accessing
your application load balancer on the HTTP protocol,
the ALB will return with a redirect
and say you need to redirect to HTTPS.
So the user comes back to the application load balancer
now on the HTTPS protocol,
and therefore it will leverage the TLS certificate
coming from the Certificate Manager.
And then once a request is going through the HTTPS protocol,
then it will be directed into your Auto Scaling group.
So let's look at how ACM integrates with the API Gateway.
But first we have to remember the endpoint types.
So we have the edge-optimized endpoint type for API Gateway.
This is when your clients are global
and the requests are going to be routed first
through CloudFront Edge locations
to improve the latency
and then sent to an API Gateway
that still lives in only one region.
You can also have the regional type of endpoints
in which clients are within the same region
as your API Gateway.
In this case, we don't have CloudFront available,
but we could still, if we wanted to,
create our own CloudFront distribution
to have more control over the caching
and the distribution strategy.
And then we have the private API Gateway endpoints
that can only be accessed
from within our VPC using an interface VPC endpoints.
And we need to use a resource policy
to define access to this API Gateway in a private mode.
So ACM makes sense for edge-optimized
and regional endpoints, so let's have a look at that.
So to integrate ACM with the API gateway,
first, we need to create a resource
in the API gateway called a custom domain name
and then we need to configure it.
So for edge-optimized endpoints,
then because the requests are routed through CloudFront,
then the TLS certificates are going to be attached
to your CloudFront distribution
and therefore the TLS certificate must be created
in the same region as CloudFront, which is us-east-I.
So therefore, your API Gateway lives in one region,
but then everything is distributed through CloudFront
and your ACM certificates
must live in the us-east-I region
because this is where CloudFront is located.
All the certificates for CloudFront are in us-east-I.
So then we set up a CNAME
or an alias record in Route 53 to be done.
And the regional endpoints, okay,
they're for clients in the same region as your API Gateway.
And therefore, because we only have an API Gateway,
then the TLS certificates must be imported on API Gateway
in the same region as the API Stage.
And therefore, in this example,
my ACM is only in ap-southeast-2.
And then we set up a CNAME or an alias record in Route 53
to point to your DNS.
And that's it.
So you've learned a lot about AWS Certificate Manager
in this lecture.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# Section: AWS Security & Encryption: KMS, SSM Parameter Store, Shield, WAF

So we have seen KMS for encryption,
but now let's look at CloudHSM.
So with KMS, AWS will manage the software for the encryption
and will have control over the encryption keys.
But with CloudHSM,
AWS will provision some encryption hardware.
It's called an HSM device, so a dedicated hardware,
which is a hardware security module.
And then we are going
to manage our own encryption keys entirely, not AWS.
So we have full control over the encryption keys.
The HSM device is going to be set up within the cloud
of AWS, but it is tamper resistant
with FIPS 140-2 Level 3 compliance, which means
that if anyone tries to access your HSM device manually,
then they're going to be stopped and blocked.
The CloudHSM device supports both symmetric
and asymmetric encryption keys.
So that means that you can have, for example, SSL
and TLS keys on top of it.
There is no free tier and to use the CloudHSM device,
you need to use the client software,
which is quite complicated and out of scope right now.
There is an integration
between Redshift and CloudHSM
if you wanted to leverage CloudHSM
for your database encryption and key managements.
CloudHSM is a really, really good candidate
if you want to implement SSE-C type
of encryption on top of S3, for example,
because you are managing your own encryption keys
and you are storing them into this CloudHSM.
So with the CloudHSM, AWS will manage your hardware,
whereas the service itself can be used on your own.
The CloudHSM client is something you have to use
to establish a connection into the CloudHSM service.
And then you are going to manage the keys overall.
So the IAM permissions are going to be used
to do a create, read, update, a delete of an HSM cluster
at a high level,
but then you're going to use your CloudHSM software
to manage the keys and manage the users
and their permissions to access the keys,
which is different from KMS
because in KMS, well, everything is managed using IAM.
Now, the CloudHSM clusters can have high availability
and they're spread across multiple AZ.
So they're HA, and this is super important to understand.
So you can have two AZs.
One is going to be replicated from another
and your HSM client can connect to either.
So how do we transparently leverage CloudHSM
within the AWS services encryption?
Well, there is an integration between CloudHSM and KMS.
How does that work?
Well, in KMS, we're going to define a KMS custom key store,
and that will be CloudHSM.
And that means we can get CloudHSM encryption for EBS,
S3, RDS and so on.
So how does that work?
Well, we create the CloudHSM cluster,
and we define a KMS custom key store that is going
to be connected to our CloudHSM cluster.
From there, if we create an RDS database instance
that has an encrypted EBS volume with KMS encryption,
well, internally this KMS encryption is going
to be leveraging encryption keys
within your CloudHSM cluster.
The benefit of doing this is number one,
we are actually using our CloudHSM cluster.
And number two, any API calls made through KMS
that reaches our cloud HSM cluster is going
to be logged in CloudTrail.
So if we compare CloudHSM and KMS,
the tendency of KMS is multi-tenant,
whereas for CloudHSM, it's single tenants.
They both have the same standard.
The master keys are three kinds on KMS, they're AWS owned,
AWS managed, and customer managed CMK.
Whereas for CloudHSM, it's only customer-managed CMK
because AWS cannot access your HSM device.
In terms of key type, it is very similar, symmetric,
asymmetric and digital signing for KMS
and symmetric, asymmetric and digital sending
and hashing for CloudHSM.
In terms of key accessibility, well,
KMS is accessible in multiple regions,
but because CloudHSM is deployed in a VPC,
you can share it across VPCs using VPC for sharing.
And so that means that it's going to be accessible
across multiple regions if you wanted to.
For cryptographic acceleration, well,
you can set up none on KMS, but with CloudHSM,
you have SSL and TLS acceleration you can use
at your load balancer level, or you can use Oracle
and TDE acceleration as well for your database.
That is Oracle based.
For access and authentication, you have IAM for KMS,
whereas CloudHSM has its own security mechanism
to manage users and their permissions and their keys.
And then finally, for high availability,
while KMS is a managed service and is always available
and CloudHSM will have multiple HSM devices
over different availability zones.
Other capability is CloudTrail and CloudWatch for KMS,
whereas we have MFS support as well for CloudHSM.
Finally, KMS is part of the free tier in AWS,
whereas CloudHSM is not.
So that's it for CloudHSM, I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 296. Web Application Firewall (WAF)
# Section: AWS Security & Encryption: KMS, SSM Parameter Store, Shield, WAF
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/18078429
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about AWS WAF,
the Web Application Firewall.
It's used to protect your web application
from common web exploits at the Layer 7.
Just a reminder Layer 7 is HTTP,
so it protects you against HTTP exploits.
Whereas as comparison Layer 4 is for TCP or UDP protocol.
So this WAF, this Web Application Firewall can be deployed
on the Application Balancer, and API gateway, CloudFront,
the AppSync GraphQL API, or Cognito user pools.
So remember, this is very important.
You remember the targets of WAF
because the exam will try to trick you,
and for example, make you deploy WAF on an NLB
but this is not possible.
So once you've deployed a firewall on these services,
you can define web ACL,
they're web access control lists, and their rules.
And so you can set a rule, for example,
to filter based on IP addresses.
So you can define an IP sets.
Each IP set can be up to 10,000 IP addresses.
And if you need more IP addresses,
you can use multiple rules for more IPs.
You can also filter based on HTTP headers, body.
You can use URI strings to protect
from the most common attacks, such as SQL injection
and cross-site scripting.
You can have size constraints to make sure
that the request are only up to, for example, two megabytes
or geo match to allow or block specific countries.
And you can even have rate-based rules
to count the occurrences of requests per IP
for DDoS protection, for example, to prevent a specific IP
from sending more than 10 requests per second.
So these web ACLs, they're regional, except for CloudFront,
where they are defined globally.
And if you see the term rule group, well,
it's a set, it's a reasonable set of rules
that you can add it to many web ACL.
So this is just to organize them.
So WAF has a really good use case.
So what if you want to get a fixed IP on our application
while using WAF with an application load balancer?
So WAF does not support the Network Load Balancer
because the NLB operates on Layer 4 and WAF is for Layer 7.
So therefore, to provide WAF, you need to have
an application load balancer.
But we know that an application balancer
does not have fixed IPs.
So to solve a problem, we can use a Global Accelerator
to get fixed IP for application,
and then enable WAF on our ALB.
So the architecture looks like this.
We have one region with an ALB and EC2 instances.
We're going to front our ALB with a Global Accelerator
to get a fixed IP for our application.
And we're going to attach a Web Application Firewall
with a WebACL on the same region
as where our application low balancer is located.
And therefore, we have achieved our target architecture.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.
