# 297. Shield - DDoS Protection
# Section: AWS Security & Encryption: KMS, SSM Parameter Store, Shield, WAF
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/18078425
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about AWS Shields.
And Shield is a service to protect yourself
from DDoS attacks.
What is DDoS?
Well, it's a distributed denial of service.
And the idea is that your infrastructure
is going to suddenly receive many, many requests
at the same time
from a lot of computers all around the world.
And so the goal of it is to overwhelm
and overload your infrastructure.
And this way your infrastructure cannot serve
your real users
and this is what it's called a distributed denial
of service.
So we can protect against it,
so we have the AWS Shield Standard service.
It's a free service,
it's already activated for every customer of AWS
and is going to give you protection from attacks
such as the SYN or UDP floods or any reflection attack
or other layer 3, or layer 4 attacks.
And if you want to get advanced protection,
you can use the AWS Shield Advanced service.
So this is an optional DDoS mitigation service.
It costs around 3,000 per month per organization.
And the idea is that you're going to get protected
against more sophisticated DDoS attacks
on Amazon EC2, Elastic Load Balancing, Amazon CloudFront,
the Global Accelerator and Route 53.
It also gives you 24/7 access
to the AWS DDoS response team.
So in case you get attacked,
you will have someone to help you
and get you along the way.
In case you are incurring higher fees
because you are also being attacked,
this Shield Advance protects you from these higher fees.
And this Shield Advance has an automatic application layer,
DDoS mitigation, and it's going to mean
that it's automatically going to create and evaluate
and deploy WAF rules to mitigate layer 7 attacks.
So automatically your web application firewall
will have rules to help you mitigate these attacks,
DDoS attacks if they happen at the layer 7, which is great.
So let's say for this lecture, I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

So now let's talk
about the AWS Firewall Manager.
So this is a service to manage all the firewall rules
in all accounts of an AWS organization.
So the idea is that you can manage rules
across many, many accounts at the same time.
So you can set a security policy,
and a security policy is a common set of security rules.
And so this could be Web Application Firewall rules,
so they apply it to the ALB, the API gateways, CloudFronts
and so on.
Or it could be Shield Advanced rules,
so for your ALB, CLB, NLB, the Elastic IP, and CloudFront.
It could be security policy to standardize security groups
for EC2, your Application Load Balancer,
and ENI resources in your VPC.
And it could be, as well,
rules for your AWS Network Firewall at the VPC level.
So this is something we haven't seen yet
or your Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall.
So the idea is that Firewall Manager allows you
to manage all your firewalls in one place.
The policies are created at the region level, okay?
And then they are applied to all the accounts
of your organization.
And on top of it,
if somehow in your organization, for example,
you create a WAF rule for an Application Load Balancer,
and somehow there's a new Application Load Balancer
being created,
then automatically the Firewall Manager
is going to apply the same rule
to this newly created ALB.
That's a feature of Firewall Manager.
So you may ask yourself,
"Well, what is the difference between WAF
and Firewall Manager and Shield?"
Well, WAF, Shield, and Firewall Manager
are used together for comprehensive protection
of your accounts.
So first you define your Web ACL rules in WAF.
And in case you need one-time protection,
then WAF is going to be the right choice for you.
But if you want to use WAF across multiple accounts
and accelerate WAF configuration
and automate the protection of new resources,
then you would manage your WAF rules
within Firewall Manager.
And Firewall Manager will just apply
all these rules to all your accounts
and all your resources automatically.
So now we also have Shield Advanced
to help you get protected against DDoS attacks.
And it has additional features on top of WAF
such as a dedicated support
from the Shield Response Team, SRT,
advanced reporting,
and also, it can automatically create WAF rules for you.
And if you're prone to frequent DDoS attacks,
then you should definitely consider
purchasing Shield Advanced.
And so Firewall Manager
can also help you deploy Shield Advanced
across all your accounts
So hopefully the distinction is pretty clear for you now.
I hope you liked this lecture,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 300. DDoS Protection Best Practices
# Section: AWS Security & Encryption: KMS, SSM Parameter Store, Shield, WAF
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/33879042
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So here is a lecture
that is more focused on the solution architecture,
and this is around DDoS protection and best practices.
So let's assume that you have this kind of architecture.
We have an auto scaling group with EC2 instances.
It's fronted by a Elastic Load Balancer,
and then your load balancer can be either exposed
by a Global Accelerator as fixed IPs,
or it could be fronted, for example, by CloudFronts.
CloudFronts can be linked to WAF,
a web application firewall, and so on.
You can have Route 53 for DNS routing.
And finally you could also have another architecture
where you have CloudFront and the API gateway.
So this is just to represent the
kind of combinations you can do.
Obviously there are more than one,
but the idea's that we're going to discuss
thanks to the letter BP1, best practice one,
best practice two, et cetera,
what the implications are
in terms of DDoS resiliency, okay?
So by using CloudFront, we are actually at the Edge.
So this slide is all about Edge location mitigation.
That means that your web application delivery
is at the Edge, and so you're going
to be protected against DDoS common attacks
by using Shield, just a normal setup of Shield's,
so SYN floods and UDB reflection.
If you use the Global Accelerator,
this is going to be able to access your application
around the world, again at the Edge.
And again, it's fully integrated
with Shield for DDoS protection.
So it's very helpful if your backend
is somehow not compatible with CloudFronts.
In this case, you would have Global Accelerator
in front of it, and so that means that no matter
what backend you have, either using CloudFront
or the Global Accelerator,
you will be fully distributed at the Edge of AWS
and the Edge location will be DDoS protected.
Also, if you use Route 53,
then the domain name resolution is global,
it's at the Edge, and you also have
a DDoS protection mechanism on your DNS.
So we understand that if we're at the Edge,
we can have a better DDoS protection.
Next, we can have the best practices for DDoS mitigation.
So first, let's look at the infrastructure layer defense.
This is BP1, BP3, and BP6.
So the idea is that by using CloudFront,
Global Accelerator, Route 53
and the Elastic Load Balancing,
we protect our Amazon EC2 instances against high traffic.
And this is the idea that by using all these services,
the traffic is going to be handled by most of them
before ever reaching our EC2 instances.
Now, if we enable our EC2 instances with auto-scaling,
that means that in case the traffic does indeed
reach our auto scaling group, we can scale automatically
to accommodate for a greater load on our application.
And if we use Elastic Load Balancing,
then the ELB is going to automatically spread
the traffic across many EC2 instances.
And so that means that each EC2 instances
will have a manageable amount of traffic onto them,
provided the fact that the auto-scaling group
of course has scaled as well.
Now at the application layer defense,
we can detect and filter malicious requests
at BP1 and BP2.
So the idea is that CloudFront is going
to serve static content, and serve it from Edge locations,
therefore protecting your backend.
And then you can use WAF on top of CloudFront,
or your application load balancers to filter
and block requests based on request signatures,
for example, you can block specific IPs,
specific request types and so on.
And if you use the WAF rate based rules,
you can automatically block the IPs of bad actors.
So you can use a bunch of managed rules on WAF
to block IPs based on reputation
or block anonymous IPs and so on.
And using CloudFront, you can block specific geographies.
The idea is that CloudFront and WAF are managed services,
and so they will take care of filtering
some requests for you, so you can be protected
against DDoS attack.
And of course using Shield Advanced,
so in case you enable it,
then it will automatically create WAF rules for you
to mitigate layer seven attacks.
So this is good for the application layer defense,
again to protect your EC2 instances
from getting any bad request or at least minimize them.
And also, how do we reduce our attack surface?
So the idea with this architecture is
that the backend AWS resources are used
to serve our application, are hidden.
So we have BP1, BP4, and BP6.
So if we use CloudFront, the API Gateway,
or Elastic Load Balancing,
we can hide our backend resources.
The attacker will never know if it's a lambda function
or EC2 instances or ECS tasks, and so on,
because we have used other things in front of them.
Also, we can set up security groups and network ACLs
to filter traffic based on specific IPs,
and elastic IPs, if we use them,
they can be protected by AWS Shield Advanced as well.
And then you can protect API endpoints themselves,
so if you use the API gateway,
then you can hide whatever backend it is,
whether it be EC2, lambda or something else.
And if you use the Edge optimized mode,
you're already global.
Otherwise you can use CloudFront plus the regional mode,
which gives you more control for DDoS protection.
And if you use WAF on top of the API gateway,
then you can get filtering of any HTTP request.
And if you set up the API gateway correctly,
you can have burst limits, you can do headers filtering,
and you can use and force API keys for your users,
therefore protecting yourself from a DDoS attack.
So hopefully this kind of architecture makes sense
and you understand the different ways you can protect
against DDoS, because the exam will ask you
to think just like that, okay?

So now let's talk about Amazon Inspector.
So Amazon Inspector is a service that allows you
to run automated security assessments on a couple of things.
First of all, on the E2 instances.
So you are going to be leveraging the Systems Manager agent
on your EC2 instances and Amazon Inspector
is going to start to assess the security
of that E2 instance.
It's going to analyze against unintended network
accessibility and also analyze the running operating system
for known vulnerabilities.
This is done continuously.
Then we have also Amazon Inspector
for your Container Images push to Amazon ECR.
For example, your Docker images.
So as your Container Images are being pushed
to Amazon ECR, they will be analyzed
by Amazon Inspector against known vulnerabilities.
And we also have Amazon Inspector for Lambda functions.
So Lambda functions, when they're deployed,
will be analyzed again
by Inspector for software vulnerabilities
in the function code and the package dependencies.
And this assessment happens
as the functions are being deployed.
So once Amazon Inspector is done doing its job,
it can report its findings
into the AWS Security Hub and also send findings
and events of these findings into Amazon EventBridge.
This gives you one way to centrally
see the vulnerabilities running on your infrastructure
and with EventBridge you can run some kind of automations.
So what does Amazon Inspector evaluate?
You have to remember, the Inspector is only
for your running EC2 instances, your Container Images
on Amazon ECR and your Lambda functions.
And it's going to do a continuous scanning
of the infrastructure only when needed.
So it's going to look
at a database of vulnerabilities, so CVE,
for package vulnerability for EC2, ECR and Lambda.
And it's going to look
at network reachability on Amazon EC2
and in case the database of CVE gets updated,
then Amazon Inspector is going to automatically
run again to make sure
that all your infrastructure is tested one more time.
Every time it will run,
a risk score is going to be associated
with all the vulnerabilities for prioritization.
So that's it for Amazon Inspector.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

Now let's talk about Macie.

and data privacy service that will use machine learning
and pattern matching to discover
and protect your sensitive data in AWS.
More specifically, it will alert you around sensitive data
such as personally identifiable information,
which is named PII.
So very simply, your PII data will be in your S3 buckets
and it will be analyzed by Macie
which will discover what data can be classified as PII.
And then will notify you
through EventBridge of the discoveries.
Then you can have integrations into an SNS topic,
Lambda functions and so on.
So Macie in this instance will be used
to find the sensitive data in your S3 buckets
and that's the only thing it will do.
It's just one click to enable it.

and that will be it.

# Section: Networking - VPC

# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's talk about CIDR or CIDRs
or Classless Inter-Domain Routing,
which I will call CIDR for the rest of this course.
So, it's a method for allocating IP addresses
and we've seen them before in this course,
because when we look at security group rules for example
and networking in AWS, we saw something like this.
So, these are my security group rules
and if we look at the source column,
here we remember we had an IP address / and then a number
and this was our first touch with CIDRs.
So, CIDRs help define IP ranges
that we've seen some very, very simple one.
So, when we have an IP address /32,
this actually represents only one IP.
And when we saw 0.0.0.0/0
then this is represented all IPs,
but there are a lot of different possibilities.
For example,
if we define 192.168.0.0/26
then this represents a range of 64 IP addresses
as you see in this slide.
So, how does CIDR work?
Well, CIDR has two components.
There's the base IP and this is an IP that is contained
in the range.
Usually it is the beginning of the range,
but it could be that it's contained in the range.
And then, so this is example, so 10.0.0.0 or 192.168.0.0.
And then the other thing is the subnet mask
and the subnet mask will define how many bits
can change in the IP.
So, we have the /0, /24 all the way to /32
and this can take two different forms.
So, if we have /8 this is equivalent
to subnet mask of 255.0.0.0
and /16 is 255.255.0.0
and so on, okay.
But the most common form we see in this course and in AWS
is the / form, okay?
So, for the rest of this course
we'll be using /8, /16 and so on.
Now, let's have a detailed look at subnet masks.
So, this is how we can define
which values can change from the base IP.
So, if we have an IP address /32,
this allows for one IP, 2 to the power of 0
and this is the IP that we have on the left hand side.
Now, if we have an IP /31,
then we allow for two different IPs.
And so we'll allow for 192.168.0.0 and then .0.1.
If we have the same IP /30,
now this goes exponentially as you can see,
we allow for 4 IPs.
So, we'll have a bigger range from .0 to .3,
then /29 allows for 8 IPs so .0 to .7.
/28 allow for 16 IPs, so .0 to .15,
then we can look at the table, okay.
So, it goes from 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 IPs to change.
So, the /24 is 256 IPs, which is 2 to the power of 8
and this is from .0 to .255.
Then if we go one step deeper,
so we go to /16, so I skipped some in the middle.
Then we allow for 2 to the power of 16 IP to change,
so 65,536.
So, as we can see the last two parts of the IPs have changed
and then /0 allows for all IPs,
so from the very beginning to the very end.
So, how do we know?
As a quick memo we know an IP is made of 4 Octets,
so the first part, the second part,
the third part and the fourth part.
And /32 means no octets can change,
/24 means the last octet can change,
/16 means the last 2 octets can change
and take different values.
/8 is the last three octets can change
and /0 is all octets can change.
So, hopefully they started making a little bit more sense
into how CIDRs work.
So, now here comes a little exercise,

Well, this is /16,

How many IPs are including to the range and so on?

If we do /17, which is a little bit less obvious.

have an IP that starts with 192, okay?

# 307. VPC Overview
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528540
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's go ahead with creating
our first VPC in AWS.
So VPC stands for Virtual Private Cloud.
And you can have multiple VPC within a single AWS region.
You could have a maximum of five per region,
but this is a soft limit, so you can increase it.
And the number of CIDRs assigned per VPC is five.
Now for each CIDR, the minimum size is /28,
so that means at least 16 IP addresses.
The maximum size is /16, which is at max
65,536 IP addresses.
And because VPC is a private resource,
only Private IPv4 ranges are allowed.
So again, as a reminder, we have this range,
that range, and that range.
Now how do we choose the range for our VPC
in terms of what types of VP are we going to assign to it?
Well, the general rule is that you can assign
whatever you want, but you should make sure
that your VPC CIDR does not overlap
with your other VPCs or other networks
or corporate networks, and the reason we do so
is that if you want to connect them together,
we want to make sure the IP addresses
of one VPC or one CIDR do not overlap
with the range of IP addresses of other networks.
So at the end of this hands-on,
we're just going to have within a region a simple VPC.
So let's get started.

the second one,

the .2, which is reserved by AWS for mapping
to Amazon provided DNS,
and this is very important,
.3, which is not used yet,

And we have .255, which is a network broadcast address.
But because AWS does not support broadcast in a VPC,
this address is reserved and cannot be used, okay?

if you need 29 IG IP addresses in a sub-net
for EC2 instances,
then you can not choose a subnet of /27

you're going to get 27 addresses,
which are less than the number 29 that we need.
So we need to choose a subnet size of /26
because this gives us 64 IP addresses in that subnet.
And then if you remove the five reserved IP addresses

which is greater than the 29 we needed, okay?

# 311. Internet Gateways & Route Tables
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528544
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay so now we're going to see how we can get
internet access into our subnets
because right now we don't know what a Public Subnet is
and what a Private Subnet is, and currently,
both our subnets do not have internet access.
So an Internet Gateway will allow resources
in a VPC to connect to the internet,
and it could be EC2 instances allowing the functions
and so on.
It will scale horizontally
and it's highly available and redundant.
So it's a really nice managed resource
and it must be created separately from a VPC.
Now one VPC can only be attached to one Internet Gateway
and vice versa and Internet Gateways on their own
do not allow internet access.
We must also edit the Route Tables to make it work.
So we'll see this in a second.
So currently we have a VPC.
We have two subnets in one EC,
so I didn't represent the other two subnets
to make this diagram as simple as possible.
We're going to create an Internet Gateway in this VPC,
and this enough will not give internet access

# 313. Bastion Hosts
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528558
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about bastion hosts
and the idea is that our users
want to access an EC2 instance that is
in a private subnet, but we as users,
we are on our computer on the public internet.
So obviously because our EC2 instance
is in a private subnet
we don't have direct internet access to it.
So the trick, or one trick at least,
is to use a bastion host.
The bastion host is an EC2 instance,
that's named bastion host, okay?
And that EC2 instance is special
because it is in a public subnet.
It has its own security group called
the bastion host security group,
then we also have a security group, of course,
for our EC2 instance in the private subnet.
Now, the idea is that the EC2 instance
in the public subnet, our bastion host,
does have access to the EC2 instance in our private subnet,
well, because everything is in our VPC.
So now to access our EC2 instance in the private subnet,
what we do is that we first connect
through SSH to the bastion host
and then connect from the bastion host,
again with SSH, to the EC2 instance in the private subnet.
And it could be one
but it could be as well, many EC2 instances.
So to summarize a bastion host is a way for us
to SSH into our private EC2 instances.
And we must put the bastion host in the public subnet.
So in terms of security group rules,
this is something that can come up with the exam,
we need to understand what we can define.
So for a bastion host perspective,
the security group must allow access
from the internet, okay?
But instead of allowing everywhere
from the internet access,
because that could be a security risk,
we can only restrict, for example,
access from the public CIDR of your corporation
or your internet access and so on.
So that we have to restrict the EC2 security group
of the bastion host as much as possible to guarantee
that only a few select IPs can access it,
because if somehow a random attacker has access
to our EC2 instance as the bastion host,
it could be a security risk for our infrastructure.
Now, in terms of the security group
of the EC2 instances in the private subnets,
well, they must allow the SSH access,
so on the port 22 again, from this time the private IP
of the bastion host
or the security group of the bastion host,
this is equivalent.
And this is because the traffic
these EC2 instances are seeing are originating
from this bastion host.
So that's it for this lecture,
I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 315. NAT Instances
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528548
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about NAT instances,
which are definitely outdated.
There is a better solution called NAT gateway
in the next lecture, but they still can appear at the exam.
So let's go and have a look at them.
So NAT means Network Address Translation,
and these NAT instances allow EC2 instances
in private subnets to connect to the internet.
To do so, the NAT instance must be launched
in a public subnet and then will connect the public subnet
and the private subnets.
There's also a setting we'll have to disable,
and we'll see this in the hands-on,
called the source/destination check,
and I'll show you this right now why.
Also, your NAT instance must
have a fixed Elastic IP attached to it.
So let's have a look.
So we have a server,
and it's a public server with a public IP, 50.60.4.10,
and we want to access it from our private subnets, okay.
So how do we establish connectivity from the private subnets
to the server?
Well, to do so, we're going to launch a NAT instance
with its own security group in a public subnet,
then what we're going to do is attach an Elastic IP
to this NAT instance,
and then we're going to edit the route tables
from the private subnet to the public subnet
to be allowed to send traffic from the EC2 instances
between the two subnets to the NAT instance.
So then the IP at the instance wants to access the server,
the public server,
but it has to go through the NAT instance.
So the request is seeing that the source IP is 10.0.0.20,
which is true, which is a private IP,
and the destination is 50.60.4.10 which the NAT instance
is smart enough to say, hey, I know you're trying
to send traffic to something else,
so let me send the traffic over to that server.
But that server has something different.
So the destination is still this IP,
but now the source IP is 12.34.56.78,
which is corresponding to the public IP of the NAT instance.
So as you can see, this network packet gets rewritten
by the NAT instance, this is what NATs do,
they rewrite network packets,
and the source IP has changed.
The server now says, hey, I know how to reply to you
because the source is me and the destination
is the public IP of your NAT instance,
and then the NAT instance will reply back the traffic
to the EC2 instance, it's smart enough to know which one
to go to, and say, hey, the source is the public server
and the destination is your private IP.
And this is why,
because there's some IPs are being rewritten,
this is why the source and destination check
must be disabled on the EC2 instance for your NAT instance.
So this is how NAT instances work at a high level.
So again, we're going to create a NAT instance
within a public subnet, and next I attach an Elastic IP
to it, and then we're going to have a route table
which allows the private instances to talk
to the NAT instance all the way
to the internet gateway and so on.
So some comment about NAT instances.
So we have a pre-configured Amazon Linux AMI available
to us, and although it's available there,
it reached its end of standard support
on December 31st, 2020.
So NAT gateways are now recommended,
and NAT instances are not highly available.
They're not resilient with out of the box setup,
so we need to create multiple ones and multiple AZs,
and maybe have an ASG, have a resilient user-data script.
It's quite complicated.
And then if you select a small instances,
then you're going to get less bandwidth
than a bigger instance.
You also must manage Security Groups and rules
on your instance.
So inbound, you must allow whatever HTTP HTTPS traffic
from the private subnets,
allow maybe SSH from your home network,
and outbound, you need to also allow some traffic outbound.
So NAT instances, they work.
This is good to see how NATs work at a high level,
and this is what this lecture is about.
We're going to set up a NAT instance in the next lecture,
but remember, they're going away and the exam will ask you

# 319. Regional NAT Gateway
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/55787777
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's have a quick chat
about regional NAT gateways or RNATs.
So it's a new type of NAT gateway that is highly available
and associated directly with your VPC.
So before, the NAT gateway had to be created
within each public subnets,
but now you just create it at the VPC level,
and then you link it to the Internet gateway.
How?
With the route table.
So you create the NAT gateway, it's in your VPC,
and you tell it that anything that goes to the Internet
should go to your Internet gateway.
The added benefit is
that now you don't need to deploy a NAT gateway per AZ,
automatically, this is shared across all the AZs.
You also don't need to maintain public subnets in your VPC
to host the regional NAT gateway.
So no risk for anyone to create resources
in the public subnet
that you didn't want to use in the first place.
Then, you link your private subnet directly
into your NAT gateway using a route table,
and you're good to go.
Your private subnet instances will have access
to the Internet through this NAT gateway.
And automatically, if you add another AZ,
another private subnet in another AZ,
then it will be detected
and the NAT gateway will scale for you.
So this simplifies solution architecture
by having one central NAT gateway per VPC
instead of creating a NAT gateway instance per AZ.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

So now let's talk about VPC Peering.
So the idea is that we can create VPCs
and in different regions, different accounts
and we want to connect them together using the AWS network.
Why we do this?
Well, we wanna make them behave
as if they were in the same network, okay?

Maybe you could have VPC in other regions

if they have overlapping CIDRs,
they will not be able to communicate.
So, VPC peerings can happen between two VPCs
and they're not transitive.
That means that each VPC
that wants to communicate with one another
must have VPC peering enabled.
So if you have a look at three VPCs right now, A, B, and C,
then we can create a peering connection between A and B.
And this is allowing you to connect them together.
And we can create another peering connection
between VPC B and C,
and again, they can communicate together.
But even though A and B, and B and C, are connected,
you still need to enable a VPC peering connection
between A and C, to have them communicate.
This is very, very, very, very important.
Finally, even though your VPC are peered with each other,
you must also make sure that you update all the route tables
in each VPC's subnets, to ensure that these two instances
in different VPC, can communicate with each other.
And we'll see this in the hands-on.

They can happen within your own accounts,

# 324. VPC Endpoints
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528556
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about VPC endpoints.
The idea is that you have services on AWS, for example,
such as DynamoDB and they are accessible publicly.
So that means that your whole infrastructure
through your NAT gateway and then your internet gateway
or just directly
through your internet gateway does access DynamoDB.
But all this traffic goes through the public internet
and you may have other services such as CloudWatch
and Amazon S3 that you also wanna access
without going through the internet.
You wanna access them privately.
So the idea is that you're going to use VPC endpoints
so that your instances don't have to go
through the public internet,
they can just go directly
through the private AWS network to these services.
So let's consider this architecture that we know already,
so we have public subnets with a NAT gateway
and it's EC2 instance, a private subnet,
and then we're going to have an internet gateway
so that we know we can access the Amazon SNS service
for example, through different ways.
So if we look at the private subnet
and the EC2 instance in it,
to access the Amazon SNS service,
the EC2 instance can go through the NAT gateway
which then goes to the internet gateway
and then accesses publicly the Amazon SNS service
and this is the same
for the EC2 instance in the public subnet,
it goes directly through the internet gateway
to the Amazon SNS service.
And this option is fine
but it costs just a lot of money because, well,
we have to go through NAT gateway, which has a cost,
and then we have to go through the internet gateway
which doesn't have a cost
but still there is obviously many hops
and it's not very efficient.
So instead, I'm just representing
the same Amazon SNS service,
but somewhere else on the diagram,
we can use a VPC endpoint.
And the idea is that the VPC endpoint is deployed
within your VPC and by doing some networking,
we can actually make the EC2 instance
in the private subnet go through the VPC endpoint
directly into the Amazon SNS service
and the network has never left AWS, which is really good.
So, every AWS service is publicly exposed,
it has public a URL,
and if you use VPC endpoints, they are powered
by something called AWS PrivateLink because you
access these services privately.
Then you can connect to any of these services
by AWS using a private network
instead of going over the public internet.
These VPC endpoints are redundant and they scale
horizontally, and they're going to remove the need
for an internet gateway or a NAT gateway
to access AWS services,
thus simplifying your network infrastructure by a lot.
So in case of issues, you need to check the DNS
settings resolution in your VPC and your route tables.
So this is the general idea behind the VPC endpoints now,
we have two types of VPC endpoints.
We have the Interface Endpoints
and these are powered by PrivateLink
and we have the Gateway Endpoints.
So the Interface Endpoints provision an ENI,
so it's a private IP address in your VPC
and this ENI is an entry point to your private AWS service.
And so for this, we must attach a security group
because there is an ENI and it supports most AWS services
if not all, and there's a cost to it, it's a cost
per hour and it's a cost per gigabyte of data processed.
So here we go, we have an EC2 instance
and a private subnet and thanks to a PrivateLink
VPC endpoint of type interface
then we can access through the ENI to the service.
And this works for every single service out there.
Now we have the Gateway Endpoint and they're special.
They provision what's called a gateway
and this has to be used as a target in a route table.
So this does not leverage IP addresses,
this is not a leverage security groups,
it's just a target in a route table
and you need to remember that.
And there are only two targets for a Gateway Endpoint,
it is Amazon S3 and DynamoDB, but the advantage
that this is free and this scales automatically
because it's only a route table access.
So, it's only for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB, remember this.
And in this instance,
we provide a VPC endpoint of type gateway
and we have access to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB.
So the question you may ask me is, hey,
if the Interface Endpoint supports everything
and the Gateway Endpoint supports Amazon S3 and DynamoDB,
should I use the Gateway
or the Interface Endpoint for Amazon S3 or DynamoDB?
Well, we have indeed two ways
of accessing Amazon S3, right?
Either with the Gateway Endpoint
or with an Interface Endpoint.
And at the exam, the Gateway is most likely going to
be the preferred solution at the exam, why?
Well, because we just have to modify a route table.
So, and your apps can access Amazon S3 free of charge,
so the cost is free for a Gateway, it scales more,
and for the Interface Endpoint,
you have a cost associated with it.
The only time where an Interface Endpoint may be preferable
over a Gateway Endpoint is
if you require access from on-premises, for example
you want private access from your on-premise data center
and we haven't seen it yet, but we can connect it
through something called site to site VPN or direct connect
or it's maybe preferable if you want to connect
from another VPC through this Interface Endpoint.
So these are advanced use cases, right?
And this is what is represented on this graph.
But most of the time
the Gateway Endpoint is going to be preferred
for Amazon S3.
Okay, that's it for this lecture,
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 326. VPC Flow Logs
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/28874566
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now, let's talk about VPC Flow Logs.
VPP flow logs allow you
to capture information from IP traffic going
into your interfaces.
So that could be at the VPC level, the subnet level,
or the elastic network interface, ENI level.
So we have three kinds of flow logs.
They're very helpful to monitor
and troubleshoot connectivity issues
happening within your VPC.
So these flow logs can be sent to Amazon S3,
CloudWatch Logs, and Kinesis Data Firehose,
and they will capture information
for also AWS managed interfaces such as ELB, RDS,
ElasticCache, Redshift, Workspaces, your net gateway,
your transit gateway, and so on.
So this is what a VPC flow log looks like.
So there is a format associated with it,
but there is a version, account ID, interface ID,
source address, destination address,
source port, destination port, protocol packets by start
and action and log status.
So this is metadata about the network packets
going into your VPC.
And you don't need to remember this at a high-level, right?
But let's have a look at
what information we can get out of these flow logs.
So the source address and the destination address
help identify problematic IP.
This is where you see if an IP is repeatedly being denied,
maybe there is something wrong with that IP,
or maybe you're being attacked by a specific IP, source port
and destination port helps you identify the probiotic ports.
Action is going to be either accept or reject.
And so it's going to say whether or not it's a success
or failure at the SG or NACL level.
And we'll see this in the very next slide.
And so this can be used the VPC logs
to do analytics on usage patterns
or detect manage behavior, port scans, and so on.
Now, to query these flow logs,
you have two ways of doing it.
The best way is to do Athena on S3,
or if you wanted to do a streaming analysis,
you could use CloudWatch logs insights.
So here are some examples
that you can have a look on your own time for flow logs.
So how do we use flow logs to troubleshoot security group
and NACL issues?
Well, we look at the action field.
So let's have a look at the typical incoming request
for your NACL and your subnet.
So remember, your NACL are stateless
and your security groups are stateful.
So what happens?
Well, if we get an inbound reject,
so we see that the inbound request from from the outside
to our EC2 instance is rejected.
That can means that either from this graph,
the NACL is refusing the request
or the security group is refusing the request.
And this makes sense, right?
But if we have a inbound accept
and an outbound reject, it can only mean a NACL issue.
Why?
Or because your security group is stateful.
And if the inbound is allowed
because of the accept, automatically the outbound
will be allowed thanks to the statefulness
of your security group.
So for outgoing request, similar analysis, right?
This is the diagram we know already.
And so if you get an outbound reject,
then you have a NACL or a security group issue.
But if you get an outbound accept and inbound reject,
then it must mean a NACL issue.
So let's have a look at a few architectures
for your VPC flow logs
so they can flow into CloudWatch logs as we know.
And then we can use something
called CloudWatch contributor insights,
for example, to find the top 10 IP addresses
that contribute to the most amount of network on your VPC
or on ENI or whatever you want.
You can also use VPC flow logs
to send them again into CloudWatch logs.
Here, we can set up a metric filter to look for example
for the SSH or the RTP protocols.
And if we realize that there's a lot more SSH
or RDP than usual, then trigger a CloudWatch alarm
and send an alert into an Amazon SNS topic
because something fishy may be happening on your network.
Or we can use a VPC flow log.
And then we send everything into an S3 bucket for storage,
and we use Amazon Athena
to analyze the VPC flow logs with SQL.
And we can even visualize that with Amazon QuickSight.
Now a little bit of security, so you need permissions
for VPC flow logs to work.
So there is an IAM service role associated
with the VPC flow logs service,
and it must have the required permissions
to publish logs to CloudWatch Logs.
So to do so, it needs the logs, create log group,
logs create log stream or logs put log events permissions,
and then these permissions together will allow the VPC
for log service through its IAM role
to send logs into CloudWatch logs without any errors.
All right, that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 328. Site to Site VPN, Virtual Private Gateway & Customer Gateway
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13528560
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's talk
about site-to-site VPN.
So the idea is that, now we have a VPC
but we may have also a structure
within the corporate data center,
and we wanna connect AWS to our corporate data center
using a private connection.
So for this, we'll have a customer gateway
on the corporation side,
and a VPN gateway on the VPC side.
And we're going to establish,
through the public internet,
a private site-to-site VPN connection.
So it's a VPN connection, so it's encrypted.
It goes over the public internet, though.
And using this, we have linked effectively
the network of our VBC
to the network of our corporate data center.
So, as such, the VPNs need two things.
First, they need a virtual private gateway, VGW.
It's a VPN concentrator on the AWS side
of the VPN connection,
and the VGW is created and attached to the VPC
from which you want to create
the site-to-site VPN connection.
It's possible for you to customize the ASN number,
if you know what that means.
The customer gateway is a CGW,
and it's an actual software
or a physical device on your side,
so on the data center side of the VPN connection,
And there's a bunch of these
that will have been tested by AWS,
so we can have a look at the list here.
So, to do a connection, it's very simple.
We have a corporate data center with a customer gateway,
and then we have our VPC with our virtual private gateway.
So, how do we set up the customer gateway device
that is on premises?
Which IP address should we use?
Well, if your customer gateway is public,
there is a public internet-routable IP address
for your customer gateway device.
Then you would use this one,
and you would establish the connectivity
between your VGW and your CGW
using the public IP of the customer gateway.
But it's possible for your customer gateway
to also be private and have a private IP.
In which case, then it is very common for it
to be behind a NAT device that has NAT-T enabled.
And then, that NAT device has a public IP, in which case,
the IP address you should use for the CGW
is the public IP of the NAT device.
And then, the site-to-site VPN connection
can be established.
I'm saying this because this can come into the exam.
And then, the second question that can come up
to the exam is that,
even though this is set up,
this site-to-site VPN connection will not work
until you enable route propagation in your VPC
within your subnets.
And then, when this is done,
then the connectivity will work.
Finally, another exam question that can come up
regarding site-to-site VPN.
If you need to ping your EC2 instances
from on-premises to AWS,
then make sure that the ICMP protocol on the inbound
of the security group is enabled.
Otherwise, I would say the connection will not work.
This is just a security group question, obviously.
But they mix it up with the site-to-site VPN
and that can be confusing, so here is some help.
Now, there's one last thing to know
about a site-to-site VPN.
It's called AWS VPN CloudHub.
So the idea is that you have your VPC with your VGW
and you have multiple customer networks,
multiple data centers, each with their own customer gateway.
So CloudHub is to provide secure communication
in between all these sites, using multiple VPN connections.
It's a low-cost hub-and-spoke model
for primary or secondary network connectivity
between different locations,
but only using the VPN.
So you would establish a site-to-site VPN
between the CGW and the one single VGW within your VPC.
And then, thanks to this connection,
then your customer networks can now communicate
with one another through that VPN connection.
Now, because it's a VPN connection,
all the traffic goes over the public internet.
So they're not connected through a private network.
They're connected through public network
but the VPN connection is encrypted, obviously.
And to set it up, super simple,
you set up multiple site-to-site VPN connection
on the same virtual private gateway,
and then you enable dynamic routing
and you configure your route tables, and you're good to go.
So that's it.
That's all you need to know for site-to-site VPN.

# 330. Direct Connect & Direct Connect Gateway
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/13531250
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's talk about Direct Connect.
And you may also see it as DX in the exam.
So it provides a dedicated private connection
from a remote network into your VPC.
So you need to set up that dedicated connection
and it is using an AWS Direct Connect location.
You also need to set up a virtual private gateway
on your VPC side to make the connectivity
between your on-premises data center and AWS.
The idea is that on the same connection,
you can access both public resources such as Amazon S3
and private resources such as EC2 instances
using the public VIF and the private VIF.
So what are the use cases for Direct Connect?
Well, you get increased bandwidth throughput.
That means that if you're working with large data sets,
it's going to be faster because it doesn't go
over the public internet.
And also you're going to have lower cost
because you're using a private connection.
Also, if you have connectivity issues
using the public internet,
while using Direct Connect,
you get a more consistent network experience again,
because it is private.
So this is especially helpful if you have applications
using real time data feeds.
Finally, it supports hybrid environments
because you have connectivity
between your on-premises data center and the cloud.
It supports both IPv4 and IPv6.
So let's look at a diagram of Direct Connect.
So we have a region,
and we want to connect it into our corporate data center.
So for this we're going to commission
an AWS Direct Connect location.
There are physical locations that you have to find,
but it's all obviously on the website of AWS,
and there's going to be a Direct Connect endpoint,
and there's going to be a customer
or partner router that you have
to rent from a customer or partner cage.
So you have two cages in this Direct Connect location.
And then on your on-premises data center,
you're going to set up a customer router with a firewall.
Now you're going to set up a private virtual interface,
so private VIF,
first to access your private resources into your VPC.
So to do so, you set up the private VIF
in between all these locations
into a virtual private gateway.
And this virtual private gateway is attached to your VPC.
And through the private VIF,
you are able to access your private subnet
with your EC2 instances.
And as you can see, all these things happen privately.
So you need to set up that connection manually.
It can take a month to set up,
but none of this goes over the public internet.
It is all a private connectivity.
The alternative is to connect to public services within AWS,
such as Amazon Glacier or Amazon S3.
And for this, you're going to set up
a public virtual interface or public VIF.
And so it goes through the same path,
but it doesn't connect into a virtual private gateway.
It connects directly into AWS.
So what if you want to connect
to one or more VPCs in different regions?
For this, you must use a Direct Connect gateway.
So we have an example where we have two regions
and they have two different VPC with two different CIDRs,
and we want to connect our on-premises data center
into both VPC.
So we're going to establish a Direct Connect connection.
Then using the private VIF, you're going to connect it
to a Direct Connect gateway.
And this gateway will have a private virtual interface
into a virtual private gateway in the first region
and another one in the second region.
So using the setup, we can start connecting to multiple VPCs
and multiple regions.
Okay, now let's discuss the connection types
for Direct Connects.
We have the option of dedicated connections
that range from one gigabits per second
up to different options, up to 400 gigabits per second.
You get a physical ethernet port
that's dedicated to a customer,
and the request is made to AWS first,
and then it's completed by an AWS Direct partner.
And then we have a hosted connection
from 50 megabits per second, 25 gigabits per second.
Here we make the connection request directly
via the AWS Direct Connect partners as well,
and the capacity can then be added or removed on demand.
Oftentime, to build these connections,
it takes over a month.
So you need to be mindful of this.
So in the exam, they will ask you questions around,
"Hey, we want to transfer some data within a week,
and we want it to be fast."
So an answer cannot be Direct Connect
because Direct Connect takes often
more than one month to establish.
So you need to look into the question
whether or not there is already a Direct Connect established
and whether or not the time to transfer the data
is less or greater than one month.
Now when you have a Direct Connect, there is no encryption.
So data in transit is not encrypted.
But it is private because it is a private connection.
And so if you wanted encryption on top of it,
you can set up Direct Connect to be alongside a VPN
to provide IPsec encrypted private connection.
So it's good to get an extra level of security,
but it's slightly more complex to put in place.
So the setup is to get the send Direct Connect location,
but then on the connection,
you're going to set up a VPN connection on top of it
to have encryption for your Direct Connect,
and therefore all the traffic
between your corporate data center to AWS
is going to be encrypted.
Now, one last thing that can come up in the exam
is around resiliency for Direct Connects.
So we have two modes of resiliency and architectures,
and you need to know them both
because they will be coming up at the exam.
You have high resiliency for critical workloads
where we set up multiple Direct Connects.
So we have two corporate data centers.
And we have two different Direct Connect location.
And this gives us some redundancy.
So in the first case, we have a private VIF here
and we have a private VIF here.
And so here we get one connection at multiple locations.
And so if one of the Direct Connect location goes down,
then at least we have some backup
Direct Connect location somewhere else.
And so this gives us high resiliency,
and this is good for critical workloads.
But if you want to get maximum resiliency
for critical workloads,
and I emphasize the word maximum
because it can come up in the exam,
then you're going to have to set up,
again, two Direct Connect locations.
But this time each Direct Connect location
will have two connections independent
to give you maximum resiliency.
So in this use case, we have four Direct Connect locations,
four connections across two locations, sorry,
going into AWS.
And so maximum resilience is achieved
by using separate connections
terminating on separate devices in more than one location.
So that's for Direct Connect,
I hope you like this lecture
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 332. Transit Gateway
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/19030446
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so if we look at
common network topologies in AWS
it can become quite complicated.
For example, you have many VPC
and you want to peer them together,
then you want to establish some VPN connections
and direct connect,
and then you have a direct connect gateway to connect
to multiple VPC at a time, and this can become
very, very complicated in terms of network topology.
So, AWS came up with the transit gateway
to solve that problem, and you're going to have
a transitive peering connection between thousands of VPC,
your on-premises data center, your site-to-site VPN,
direct connects in a hub-and-spoke star connection.
So let's have a diagram.
We have transit gateway in the center
and you can connect multiple VPCs through
the transit gateway.
So in this example, we don't need to peer the VPCs together,
they are connected transitively through the transit gateway.
So in this example, all the VPCs can talk to each other.
But also, you can connect a direct connect gateway
to the transit gateway,
so it shows you have a direct connect connection
directly in to many different VPC.
Or if you are preferring site-to-site VPN
and VPN connections, you can connect your customer gateway
and your VPN connection into your transit gateway.
Again, one more time, giving you access to all these VPC
as part of the transit gateway.
So this really solves some network problems.
It's a regional resource and it can work cross-region,
and you can share your transit gateway across accounts
by using the resource access manager.
You can also peer transit gateways across region.
So, how do you define who can talk to what?
Well, you need to create route tables
for your transit gateway to limit which VPC
can talk to another, which connection have access
to each other and so on.
So, you get full control over the routing of all the traffic
within the transit gateway to give you network security.
So, as I said, it works with direct connect gateway
and VPN connections, and it is the only service in AWS
that supports IP multicast, so if you see IP multicast
at the exam, just know that it is transit gateway
you have to use.
So, another use case for transit gateway is to increase
the bandwidth of your site-to-site VPN connection
using ECMP.
So, it's quite technical but the question can come up
in the exam.
So, ECMP means equal-cost multi-path routing.
It's a routing strategy to allow to forward a packet
over multiple best path.
And the use case, as I said, is to create
multiple site-to-site VPN connections
to increase the bandwidth of your connection
to AWS using a site-to-site VPN.
So, let's take this example where we have a transit gateway
and we have four VPCs attached to our transit gateway,
and we have a corporate data center that is connected
using site-to-site VPN to a transit gateway.
So when you establish a site-to-site VPN connection
there are actually two tunnels, one going forward
and one going back.
When you are connecting such a VPN into a VPC directly,
both of these tunnels are used as part of one connections,
but when using the transit gateway
two tunnels can be used at a time,
so this is why you see two lines in this diagram.
But with transit gateway,
you can have multiple site-to-site VPN
so you can create a second site-to-site VPN attachment
and into your transit gateway,
so this creates four tunnels.
And so, when you have four tunnels of site-to-site VPN,
you are increasing the throughput of your connection
which is something you cannot do if you were to connect
your corporate data center directly into a VPC.
So, if you do a VPN to a virtual private gateway,
you get one tunnel, in fact one connection into one VPC,
and this connection gives you 1.25 Gbps
as the maximum throughput, and you are limited.
And in this case, a VPN connection is made of two tunnels.
But if you are using a VPN into a transit gateway,
you get one site-to-site VPN into many VPC
because they're all connected transitively
to the same transit gateway.
And also, one site-to-site VPN connection
gives you 2.5 Gbps thanks to ECMP,
because the two tunnels are going to be used
through that strategy.
But also, you can add more site-to-site VPN connections
into transit gateway, for example two or three,
to double or triple your throughputs
through ECMP.
So this is an exam question you need to know.
Obviously when you do the setup,
you're going to have to pay for each GB of data
going through the transit gateway,
so there's an added cost to this performance optimization.
Finally, you can share your direct connect connection
between multiple accounts, again, using the transit gateway.
How do we do this?
Well, we're going to establish a direct connect connection
between your corporate data center
and a direct connect location,
and then we're going to set up a transit gateway
into both VPCs in two different accounts, okay?
So this is something we can do with the transit gateway.
And then, we connect the direct connect location
into direct connect gateway and connect that gateway
into the transit gateway.
And what this just allowed us to do is to share
a direct connect connection between multiple accounts
and multiple VPC, which is very handy
thanks to the transit gateway.
Okay?
So all these sort of architectures can come up in the exam
so make sure you're familiar with understanding
how they work, and that's it for me,
I will see you in the next lecture.

# 333. VPC Traffic Mirroring
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/28874610
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So here is a very cool security feature
called the VPC, Traffic Mirroring.
The idea is that we want to capture
and inspect network traffic in our VPC,
but to do it in a non-intrusive manner.
So to do so, we want to route the traffic
to security appliances that we manage.
And to do so, we're going to capture the traffic,
so we're going to define
which are the source ENIs
we want to capture the traffic from.
And then the targets,
so where do we want to send that traffic to,
our own ENIs or maybe a Network Load Balancer.
So to do an example.
So we have an EC2 instance
and we have an Elastic Network Interface,
so an ENI attached to it
and works really well.
Our EC2 instance is accessing the internet
and is being accessed.
And so we get a lot of inbound and outbound traffic
on the ENI to the EC2 instance.
But we wanted to analyze our traffic.
So to do so we're going to set up a Load Balancer
and behind this Network Load Balancer,
we're going to have an auto scaling group of EC2 instances
that will have some security software on it.
Now we want to be able to capture
all the traffic from Source A
without disrupting the functioning of Source A.
So to do so, we're going to set up a VPC traffic mirroring,
and optionally, we can have a filter,
if you want you to get just some information,
not everything.
And with this traffic mirroring feature,
all the traffic sent to the ENI or Source A
is also going to be sent to our Network Load Balancer.
So our Source A,
our EC2 instance is still working fine.
It still doesn't know what's happening,
but on top of it,
the traffic is being mirrored.
So hence the name, Traffic Mirroring,
into our Network Load Balancer.
And from there, we can analyze the traffic itself.
And this applies not just to one source,
but to multiple sources.
So if you had a second EC2 instance with another ENI,
yet again, we can mirror the traffic
into our Network Load Balancer.
So how does that work?
We need to have the source
and the targets to be in the same VPC,
or it could be across different VPC,
and if we have enabled VPC Peering.
So the use cases for VPC traffic mirroring
is going to be around content inspection,
threat monitoring, or troubleshooting
from a networking perspective, okay.
It's very hard to demonstrate this in a demo,
but this diagram should be enough.
So hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# 334. IPv6 for VPC
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/26099590
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So we've talked a lot
about IPv4 in this course,
but now let's talk about IPv6.
So why?
Well, because IPv4 was designed
to provide 4.3 billion addresses at the time of creation.
And engineers who invented this protocol never thought
that they would be all used,
but it turns out that very, very soon,
they will all be exhausted.
And so therefore, there needs to be a new scheme of IPs,
and this is IPv6, which is a successor of IPv4.
So IPv6 is designed to provide, and wait for it,
3.4 times 10 at the power of 38 unique IP addresses.
So this is a lot of IP addresses.
And every IPv6 address in AWS is going to be public
and internet-routable.
So the format is x.x.x.x, eight times,
where x is hexadecimal,
where the range can be from 0000 to ffff.
So you don't need to know exactly how an IPv6 is formed,
okay, but these are some examples of IPv6.
I'm not going to linger on it.
Okay, you can have a look,
but what's important for you is to just see one
and say, "Oh, okay, this looks like an IPv6."
And IPv6 can take multiple forms.
Okay, so why am I talking about IPv6?
Well, because we can enable IPv6 support in our VPC.
So IPv4 can never be disabled
for your VPC and subnets, okay?
But you can enable IPv6 that are public IP addresses
to operate in dual-stack mode.
That means that your EC2 instances
when launched in your VPC will get
at least a private internal IPv4 and a public IPv6,
and they can communicate using either IPv4 or IPv6
to the internet through an internet gateway.
So let's take an example.
Our EC2 instance has a private IP as an IPv6,
which is by default public.
And then if he wants to access the internet,
it can do so through internet gateway.
So internet gateway do provide connectivities
for IPv4 and IPv6.
And then my EC2 instance will be publicly accessible
in this case because it has a public IPv6 address,
and the internet gateway
would provide internet connectivity.
So here is an exam scenario for you,
so around IPv6 troubleshooting.
So as you know, IPv4 cannot be disabled
for your VPC and subnets.
And so if you have an IPv6-enabled VPC,
and you cannot launch an EC2 instance in your subnets,
then it's not because the instance cannot acquire an IPv6
because the space is actually very, very large,
and there will be enough IPv6s for your EC2 instances.
It's because there are no available IPv4 left
in your subnets.
And the solution for this is to create an IPv4 CIDR
in your subnet.
So let's take collect this VPC,
It has an IPv4 space and so also an IPv6 space.
So we keep on launching EC2 instances
that will get private IPv4 and public IPv6.
So we launch them, we launch them, we launch them,
and then once we have exhausted the space of IPv4,
if a user tries to create a new EC2 instance,
it will get an error, not because the IPv6 ran out,
but because the IPv4 space within our subnets
or our VPC ran out,
in which case, well, what we do is that we add a new CIDR
within our VPC and our subnets,
and therefore, we can start launching new EC2 instances
that will get a different IPv4 address range for the IP.

# 336. Egress Only Internet Gateway
# Section: Networking - VPC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-solutions-architect-associate-saa-c03/learn/lecture/28874662
# Caption: en_US (manual)

And now let's talk about
egress-only internet gateways.
So they're used only for IPv6 traffic,
and they're similar to a NAT gateway,
but for IPv6.
So NAT gateway is IPv4,
but egress-only internet gateway is for IPv6.
So what do they do?
Well, they allow instances in your VPC outbound connections
over IPv6 while preventing the internet
to initiate an IPv6 connection to your instances.
And to do so, you must update your route tables.
So let's have an example.
We have the internet,
our VPC with a public subnet or private subnet.
And so this EC2 instance can access
the internet through the internet gateway
and can also have the internet initiate a connection
to the instance using IPv6,
because it's connected to the internet gateway
and it's in the public subnet.
Now we don't want that.
What we want is just outbound connections.
So let's consider an EC2 instance in a private subnet,
so it doesn't have an internet gateway,
that makes the subnet private.
And we're going to create an egress-only internet gateway.
So what's going to happen is that now
the EC2 instance in the private subnet
will be able to access the internet over IPv6
through the egress-only internet gateway,
but the internet will not be able to initiate
a connection from the internet to the EC2 instance.
So to summarize, here is a diagram
of how IPv6 routing works.
So let's consider a VPC with IPv6.
We have a public subnet, we have a private subnet,
so they both have IPv4 and IPv6 obviously in them.
And so again, if we consider a web server
accessing the internet,
it can do it over IPv4 and IPv6 through an internet gateway.
And so the route table for your public subnet
is going to have the first line to be local
for the local IPv4 and the local IPv6 traffic.
Okay, these are within the CIDRs of your subnets
or your VPC,
and then anything else,
so 0.0.0/0, this is the everything IPv4,
and the ::/0 is the everything IPv6,
go through the internet gateway,
which allows your web server to access the internet.
So this should make sense.
And this is how we enable IPv6 and IPv4 both ways
in a public subnet.
But if you consider a private subnet,
your server again has a private IPv4 and also an IPv6.
And so how do we make sure that this server
can access the internet, but not be accessed?
Well, you know already that for IPv4
we need to use a NAT gateway.
So the server connects to the NAT gateway, okay,
and the NAT gateway then connects to the internet gateway
and then accesses the internet over IPv4.
And for IPv6, we know we need to use
an egress-only internet gateway.
So IPv6, the server connects
to the egress-only internet gateway
to the internet over IPv6.
Now your route table looks a little bit different.
Again, the first two lines are the same,
but then your NAT gateway ID is a target for 0.0.0.0/0.
So this is all IPs' IPv4.
And then the fourth line is ::/0,
which represents a target
to the egress-only internet gateway,
because this is a target for the IPv6 type of traffic, okay?
So this should make sense.
And then if you have this in mind,
then you understand exactly the difference
between an internet gateway, a NAT gateway,
and an egress-only internet gateway.
So that's it.
I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# 339. VPC Section Summary
# Section: Networking - VPC

So this has been quite a long

lots of new concepts
so take your time and don't be afraid
if you didn't understand all of it, just get back to it.
But let's summarize what we learned.
So a CIDR is an IP range.
A VPC is a Virtual Private Cloud,
which is working for IPv4 and IPv6.
Subnets are tied to an AZ in which we define CIDRs
and we have public and private subnets.
So how do we have a public subnets?
Well, we attach an internet gateway
and then we create a route
from the public subnet to the Internet Gateway.
And this provides IPv4 and IPv6 internet access if enabled.
Now, route tables, they would be edited
to have route to the Internet Gateway,
the VPC peering connections, the VPC endpoints and so on.
And they're key to make sure
that the network flows within our VPC.
The bastion host was a public EC2 instance
that we were able to SSH into.
And then this instance had SSH connectivity
to other EC2 instances in private subnets.
That's what it's called the bastion host.
NAT instances was an EC2 instance deployed
in a public subnets to give internet access
to EC2 instances in private subnets.
It is old, it is getting deprecated
and you need to disable the source destination check flag
for it to work and also edit your security group rules.
So we have the NAT Gateway instead, which is much better.
It's managed by AWS.
It provides scalable internet access
to private EC2 instances
when the target of your request is an IPv4 address.
Next, NACL.
So they were network SELs
and they were firewall rules
to define inbound and outbound access at the subnet level.
And don't forget about ephemeral ports in its...
NACL are stateless,
so inbound and outbound rules are always evaluated.
Whereas security group rules are stateful.
That means that if the inbound is allowed,
the outbound is automatically allowed and vice versa.
And security group rules are applied
at the EC2 instance level.
VPC peering was very helpful to connect two VPCs together
and only if they have non-overlapping CIDRs.
And VPC peering connections are non-transitive
so if you need to connect three VPCs together,
you need to have three VPC peering connections.
VPC endpoints are allowing us to get private access
to AWS services such as Amazon S3, DynamoDB,
CloudFormation, SSM, whatever you want within the VPC.
We saw they were gateway endpoints
for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB,
and all the rest was interface endpoints.
VPC Flow Logs was the way for us to get some log level
of metadata around all the packets within our VPC,
and we had some information
around the accept and the reject traffic.
Now, VPC Flow Logs can be created at the VPC subnet
or ENI level,
and they can be analyzed and sent to Amazon S3
and then analyze using Athena,
or they can be sent to CloudWatch logs
and then analyze using CloudWatch Log Insights, for example.
Now, to connect your VPC to your data center,
you have two options.
The first one is a site-to-site VPN.
And so to do a site-to-site VPN is a VPN connection
over the public internet
in which we have to create a virtual private gateway on AWS
and a customer gateway on your data center.
And then you establish the VPN connection.
And then we saw that
if we establish multiple VPN connections
using the same virtual private gateway,
then we could use VPN CloudHub
to have a hub and spoke VPN model to connect our sites.
The second way to connect
to our data center was to use Direct Connect.
So this time the connection is completely private,
it does not go over the public internet,
but it's takes time to establish.
You need to hook your own data center
to a Direct Connect location for it to work.
So it's more involved, but it's more secure
and has a more stability onto the connection.
Now, Direct Connect Gateway was to set up a Direct Connect
to many VPCs in different AWS regions.
We saw PrivateLink
or VPC endpoint services, which is to connect privately
to services within your VPC that you have created yourselves
to customer VPC.
And the cool thing about it
is that it doesn't require VPC peering,
or the public internet, or NAT Gateway or round tables.
It's only used or mostly used
with a Network Load Balancer and an ENI.
And this allows us to expose a service
within our VPC to hundreds or thousands of customer VPCs
without exposing your network.
ClassicLink is to connect EC2-Classic instances privately
to your VPC, but it's going to be deprecated very soon too.
Transit Gateway is a transitive peering connection
for your VPC, VPN and Direct Connect,
and it has this fact that everything can flow through it,
which is quite nice.
Traffic Mirroring is to copy network traffic

a set of multiple data centers
that are geographically located within one another,

by using the private IP they will go over the network

Well, because the traffic has to leave via AWS network
and go back in for our two instances to communicate
and so AWS will charge us for that.
Instead, if we are using a private IP,

because we're now using the internal AWS network

Next, let's consider another region

can be quite expensive.

from this very simplified slide?
The first thing is that you should use a private IP

if you want to have good savings, okay,
and better network performance,

how we can optimize our networking costs

That means from AWS to the outside.
An ingress traffic is inbound traffic.
That means from the outside to AWS
which is typically free.

as much internet traffic as possible
within AWS to minimize the costs.

and we run an application in our corporate data center.

only 50 kilobytes to the user.
In that case,
the egress traffic is going to be really, really high.

maybe over the internet, right?
But if we make a smart choice,
we could move our application directly into the AWS cloud

In this case, if we're very smart

or any third party software repository

# 342. Disaster Recovery in AWS

So disaster recovery

on disaster recovery, and as a solutions architect,

as simple as possible for you.
So what is a disaster?
Well, it's any event that has a negative impact
on the company's business continuity or finances.
And so disaster recovery is about preparing
and recovering from these disasters.
So what kind of disaster recovery can we do on AWS
or in general?
Well, we can do on-premise to on-premise.

another data center maybe in Seattle.
And so this is traditional disaster recovery,
and it's actually very, very expensive.
Or we can start using the cloud
and do on-premise as a main data center.
And then if we have any disaster, use the cloud.

or if you're just all in the cloud,

and that would be a full cloud type of disaster recovery.
Now, before we do disaster recovery,
we need to define two key terms,

The first one is called RPO, Recovery Point Objective,
and the second one is called RTO, Recovery Time Objective.
